points: Column with 12 sieve trays operated at 101 kilopascals and a reflux ratio of 3.0
Feed ethanol mole fraction 0.10; distillate ethanol mole fraction 0.82
Mean Murphree tray efficiency 64 % with a standard deviation of 5 %
Tray model prediction 58 % with a prediction uncertainty of 6 %
No weeping was detected and no entrainment was detected under the stated conditions
definitions: Murphree tray efficiency = the actual change in vapour composition across a tray divided by the change that equilibrium with the liquid leaving the tray would give
mole fraction = the amount of a component divided by the total amount of all components in the same mixture
standard deviation = the spread of the individual tray values about their mean
prediction uncertainty = the standard deviation of the model estimate under the stated input ranges
limits: Efficiency values apply to the ethanol and water system at the stated reflux ratio and pressure; foaming systems are outside the tested scope
figures: Fig. 1: Murphree tray efficiency by tray position, with the model prediction
prose: Tray efficiency was measured in a laboratory sieve-tray column charged with the ethanol and water system. The column held 12 sieve trays and ran at 101 kilopascals with a reflux ratio of 3.0. Vapour and liquid samples were drawn at each tray after the compositions had settled, and each sample was analysed in duplicate by the same operator on the same instrument. Feed ethanol mole fraction (the amount of ethanol divided by the total amount of all components in the mixture) was 0.10. The distillate ethanol mole fraction reached 0.82 at the stated reflux ratio. Murphree tray efficiency, the actual change in vapour composition across a tray divided by the change that equilibrium with the liquid leaving the tray would give, averaged 64 % across the column (standard deviation 5 %, the standard deviation being the spread of the individual tray values about their mean). Fig. 1 shows the efficiency by tray position. The tray model prediction was 58 %, and the prediction uncertainty, the standard deviation of the model estimate under the stated input ranges, was 6 %. The prediction sits below the measured mean at every tray position, and the gap between prediction and measurement is widest near the feed tray. The entrainment term of the model carries the gap, because the model holds entrainment at a fixed fraction of the vapour flow while the measured compositions track a falling entrainment rate up the column. No weeping was detected at the stated vapour rates, and no entrainment was detected by the tracer test at the column top. Hydraulic limits do not explain the gap. For the ethanol and water system at the stated reflux ratio and pressure, design calculations that use the measured mean efficiency rest on a firmer basis than calculations that use the model value, and foaming systems are outside the tested scope.

points: Packed bed of activated carbon, bed length 25 centimetres, bed void fraction 0.40, bed temperature 298 kelvin
Feed gas with a carbon dioxide fraction of 15 % in nitrogen
Breakthrough time 42 minutes at the stated feed conditions
Adsorption capacity 2.8 moles per kilogram of adsorbent, standard deviation 0.2, mean of 3 runs
Capacity retained 92 % after 6 regeneration cycles
definitions: breakthrough time = the time at which the outlet carbon dioxide fraction first rises above the detection threshold of the analyser
adsorption capacity = the amount of carbon dioxide held by the bed at saturation divided by the mass of adsorbent
standard deviation = the spread of the run values about their mean
bed void fraction = the fraction of the bed volume not occupied by solid
limits: Capacity values apply to dry feed gas; humid feed gas is outside the tested scope
figures: Fig. 1: outlet carbon dioxide fraction against time for the packed bed
prose: Breakthrough of carbon dioxide through a packed bed of activated carbon was measured at a bed temperature of 298 kelvin. The bed length was 25 centimetres, and the bed void fraction, the fraction of the bed volume not occupied by solid, was 0.40. Feed gas entered the bed with a carbon dioxide fraction of 15 % in nitrogen at a steady flow, and the outlet fraction was recorded by a single analyser from the start of each run. Fig. 1 shows the outlet fraction against time. Breakthrough time, the time at which the outlet carbon dioxide fraction first rises above the detection threshold of the analyser, was 42 minutes at the stated feed conditions. Adsorption capacity, the amount of carbon dioxide held by the bed at saturation divided by the mass of adsorbent, was 2.8 moles per kilogram of adsorbent (standard deviation 0.2 moles per kilogram, the standard deviation being the spread of the run values about their mean, over 3 runs). The capacity rests on the full area above the breakthrough curve, and the curve shape near breakthrough is steep, which keeps the unused fraction of the bed short. Regeneration under vacuum restored the bed between runs, and capacity retained after 6 regeneration cycles was 92 % of the first-cycle value. The retained capacity after cycling sits within the run-to-run spread of fresh beds, and no progressive loss was detected across the cycles under the stated regeneration conditions. The outlet record carries a flat opening stretch before the rise, and the flat stretch matches the passage of feed gas through the void space ahead of the adsorption front. Front movement through the bed is steady rather than dispersed, and the steep front keeps the mass transfer zone short relative to the bed length. For dry feed gas at the stated temperature and feed fraction, the bed holds the stated capacity at breakthrough, and humid feed gas is outside the tested scope.

points: Seeded cooling crystallization of an aqueous potassium nitrate solution; seed mass 2.5 grams per litre of solution
Cooling rate 0.3 kelvin per minute to a final temperature of 283 kelvin
Crystal yield 68 % of the salt dissolved at charge
Mean crystal size 240 micrometres with a standard deviation of 35 micrometres
Product purity 99.2 % by mass
Unseeded baseline yield 47 % under the same cooling programme
definitions: crystal yield = the mass of crystals recovered divided by the mass of salt dissolved at charge
mean crystal size = the arithmetic mean of the measured crystal diameters in the recovered product
standard deviation = the spread of the measured diameters about their mean
limits: Yield and size values apply to the stated cooling programme and seed loading; other salts are outside the tested scope
figures: Fig. 1: crystal size distribution for the seeded batch
prose: Seeded cooling crystallization of an aqueous potassium nitrate solution was run in a stirred batch crystallizer. Seed mass was 2.5 grams per litre of solution, added at the point of first saturation. The cooling rate was 0.3 kelvin per minute, held from the saturation point to a final temperature of 283 kelvin. Agitation held the crystals in suspension without visible breakage, and samples for size measurement were taken from the discharge slurry. Crystal yield, the mass of crystals recovered divided by the mass of salt dissolved at charge, was 68 %. The unseeded baseline yield under the same cooling programme was 47 %, and the baseline batches nucleated late in the cooling ramp with a wide spread of crystal sizes. Mean crystal size, the arithmetic mean of the measured crystal diameters in the recovered product, was 240 micrometres (standard deviation 35 micrometres, the standard deviation being the spread of the measured diameters about their mean). Fig. 1 shows the size distribution for the seeded batch. The distribution is single-peaked, and no secondary nucleation peak was detected in the fine end of the distribution under the stated agitation conditions. Product purity was 99.2 % by mass, with mother liquor inclusions carrying the impurity load. Seeding moves nucleation from a single uncontrolled event to the seed surface, and the yield gain over the baseline sits with the longer growth period that early seeding opens. Recovered crystals were washed with a small volume of chilled saturated solution and dried under vacuum before weighing, and the wash procedure was held identical across seeded and baseline batches. Size measurement used the same sieve stack and the same operator for every batch, and broken or twinned crystals were counted under a single stated rule. For the stated cooling programme and seed loading, the seeded batch gives the stated yield and size, and other salts are outside the tested scope.

points: Titanium dioxide catalyst loading 0.5 grams per litre
Initial dye concentration 20 milligrams per litre
Dye removal 87 % after 120 minutes of irradiation
Apparent rate constant 0.017 per minute from a first-order fit
Removal in the dark adsorption control 9 %; removal under irradiation with no catalyst 4 %
Activity retained 81 % after 5 reuse cycles
definitions: dye removal = the fall in dye concentration divided by the initial dye concentration
apparent rate constant = the rate constant obtained from a first-order fit to the concentration record, a model output rather than a measured quantity

figures: Fig. 1: dye concentration against irradiation time, with the two control records
prose: Photocatalytic degradation of a dye solution was measured in a stirred reactor under a fixed lamp. Titanium dioxide catalyst loading was 0.5 grams per litre, and the initial dye concentration was 20 milligrams per litre. The suspension was stirred in the dark until adsorption settled before the lamp was switched on, and samples were filtered before analysis by the same procedure at every sampling point. Fig. 1 shows the concentration record. Dye removal, the fall in dye concentration divided by the initial dye concentration, reached 87 % after 120 minutes of irradiation. The apparent rate constant, the rate constant obtained from a first-order fit to the concentration record and a model output rather than a measured quantity, was 0.017 per minute. Removal in the dark adsorption control was 9 %, and removal under irradiation with no catalyst was 4 %. Adsorption and direct photolysis together account for a small share of the removal, and the gap between the controls and the full record sits with the irradiated catalyst. The first-order fit tracks the record closely over the opening stretch and drifts late in the run, where the falling concentration leaves fewer dye molecules near the catalyst surface. Activity retained after 5 reuse cycles was 81 % of the first-cycle removal, with the catalyst recovered by filtration and washed between cycles. No abrupt activity loss was detected between cycles under the stated recovery procedure. Lamp output was checked against a reference cell before each run, and the reactor geometry, stirring rate, and sampling positions were held fixed across the catalyst record and the two controls. Sample handling in the dark after withdrawal kept post-sampling reaction out of the record, and every concentration point rests on the same calibration line. For the stated lamp spectrum and the stated dye, the catalyst holds the stated removal and rate, and effluents with competing light absorbers are outside the tested scope.

points: Goal: tune a proportional-integral-derivative loop for a temperature process and obtain a stated response to a set point step
Process model: first-order lag with a time constant of 4.5 minutes, a dead time of 1.2 minutes, and a process gain of 1.8
Tuned settings: controller gain 3.4, integral time 2.4 minutes, derivative time 0.60 minutes
Set point step 10 % of span
Closed-loop result: overshoot 12 % of the step and a settling time of 9 minutes, with no steady-state offset detected
definitions: PID = proportional-integral-derivative, a controller that acts on the error, the accumulated error, and the rate of change of the error
time constant = the time a first-order process needs to complete the characteristic share of its total change after a step input
dead time = the delay between a change in the input and the first movement of the output
process gain = the change in output divided by the change in input, each at steady state
settling time = the time after a step at which the output enters the stated tolerance band about the set point and stays inside the band
overshoot = the peak excursion of the output beyond the set point, divided by the step size
limits: The settings apply to the stated process model; a process with a longer dead time relative to its lag is outside the worked scope
prose: This tutorial tunes a PID (proportional-integral-derivative) loop, a controller that acts on the error, the accumulated error, and the rate of change of the error. You start from a process model, apply a stated tuning rule, and finish with settings you can check against a recorded step response. The outcome to expect is a response that overshoots modestly and settles without offset. Audience: you need a first-order process model and a way to record the loop response. The process model for the worked example is a first-order lag with a time constant of 4.5 minutes, the time constant being the time a first-order process needs to complete the characteristic share of its total change after a step input. Dead time, the delay between a change in the input and the first movement of the output, is 1.2 minutes. Process gain, the change in output divided by the change in input with each at steady state, is 1.8. Enter the three model values into the tuning rule for a lag with a short dead time. The rule returns a controller gain of 3.4, an integral time of 2.4 minutes, and a derivative time of 0.60 minutes. Warning: load the integral term only after the loop is closed and tracking, because an integral term that accumulates during a long manual period drives the output hard at the switch. Apply a set point step of 10 % of span and record the response. Overshoot, the peak excursion of the output beyond the set point divided by the step size, is 12 % of the step. Settling time, the time after a step at which the output enters the stated tolerance band about the set point and stays inside the band, is 9 minutes. No steady-state offset was detected in the recorded response under the stated settings. Check the result by comparing the recorded overshoot and settling time with the values the tuning rule predicts for the model; a response far outside the prediction points to a wrong model value, most often the dead time. The settings apply to the stated process model; a process with a longer dead time relative to its lag is outside the worked scope.

points: Goal: compute the available net positive suction head for a pump drawing water from an open tank and compare the value with the pump requirement
Atmospheric pressure head 10.3 metres of water
Vapour pressure head 0.43 metres; static suction lift 2.0 metres; suction line friction loss 1.1 metres
Available head 6.8 metres from the stated terms
Required head from the pump curve 4.5 metres; margin 2.3 metres
definitions: NPSH = net positive suction head, the total head at the pump inlet measured above the vapour pressure head of the liquid
available head = the NPSH the suction layout delivers at the stated flow
required head = the NPSH the pump needs at the stated flow, read from the pump curve
static suction lift = the vertical distance from the liquid surface in the tank to the pump centreline
limits: The calculation holds for the stated liquid temperature and suction layout; a hotter liquid or a longer suction line is outside the worked scope
prose: This worked example computes the available NPSH (net positive suction head, the total head at the pump inlet measured above the vapour pressure head of the liquid) for a pump drawing water from an open tank. You finish with a margin you can compare directly with the pump requirement. Audience: you need the suction layout, the liquid temperature, and the pump curve. Inputs first. Atmospheric pressure head at the tank surface is 10.3 metres of water. Vapour pressure head at the stated temperature is 0.43 metres. Static suction lift, the vertical distance from the liquid surface in the tank to the pump centreline, is 2.0 metres. Suction line friction loss at the stated flow is 1.1 metres. Subtract the vapour pressure head, the lift, and the friction loss from the atmospheric head. The available head, the NPSH the suction layout delivers at the stated flow, is 6.8 metres. Required head, the NPSH the pump needs at the stated flow and read from the pump curve, is 4.5 metres. The margin of available head over required head is 2.3 metres. What the result shows: the layout delivers more head than the pump needs at the stated flow, and the margin absorbs small errors in the friction estimate. Check the arithmetic by adding the loss terms back to the available head; the sum returns the atmospheric head. Warning: the margin shrinks fast as the liquid warms, because vapour pressure head climbs with temperature while the other terms barely move. Recheck the vapour pressure head at the highest temperature the tank reaches before accepting the layout. A layout that fails the comparison cavitates at the impeller inlet, and cavitation shows first as noise, vibration, and a falling discharge head before any visible damage appears. Tank level matters in the same direction: a falling level raises the lift term and eats the margin from the other side, and a low-level alarm set with the margin in mind guards both failure paths. The calculation holds for the stated liquid temperature and suction layout; a hotter liquid or a longer suction line is outside the worked scope.

points: Goal: size a shell-and-tube exchanger for a stated duty and check the selected area against a fouling allowance
Duty 850 kilowatts; the hot stream enters at 363 kelvin and leaves at 323 kelvin
The cold stream enters at 293 kelvin and leaves at 313 kelvin
End temperature differences 50 kelvin and 30 kelvin; log mean temperature difference 39.1 kelvin
Overall heat transfer coefficient 0.620 kilowatts per square metre per kelvin
Clean area 35 square metres; fouling correction factor 0.92; selected area 38 square metres
definitions: LMTD = log mean temperature difference, the driving force for heat transfer averaged over the exchanger length for the stated terminal temperatures
overall heat transfer coefficient = the heat flow per unit area per unit temperature difference across the tube wall and the films on both sides
fouling correction factor = the fraction of the clean coefficient expected to remain in service after fouling deposits form
limits: The sizing holds for the stated terminal temperatures and a single-pass arrangement; a changed temperature programme is outside the worked scope
prose: This tutorial sizes a shell-and-tube exchanger from a stated duty and four terminal temperatures. You finish with a selected area and a fouling check. Audience: you need stream temperatures, a duty, and a coefficient estimate for the fluids in question. Inputs first. Duty is 850 kilowatts. The hot stream enters at 363 kelvin and leaves at 323 kelvin. The cold stream enters at 293 kelvin and leaves at 313 kelvin. Compute the driving force at each end of the exchanger. The end temperature differences are 50 kelvin at the hot inlet end and 30 kelvin at the hot outlet end. The LMTD (log mean temperature difference, the driving force for heat transfer averaged over the exchanger length for the stated terminal temperatures) is 39.1 kelvin. The overall heat transfer coefficient, the heat flow per unit area per unit temperature difference across the tube wall and the films on both sides, is 0.620 kilowatts per square metre per kelvin. Divide the duty by the product of the coefficient and the LMTD. Clean area is 35 square metres. Apply the fouling allowance before selecting a shell. The fouling correction factor, the fraction of the clean coefficient expected to remain in service after fouling deposits form, is 0.92. Selected area is 38 square metres. Tube count and shell diameter follow from the selected area under the stated tube geometry and pass arrangement. What the result shows: the selected area carries the duty at the fouled coefficient, with the allowance held in area rather than in a higher clean coefficient. Check the sizing by multiplying the fouled coefficient, the selected area, and the LMTD; the product returns the duty within rounding. Warning: a temperature cross, where the cold outlet passes the hot outlet, breaks the LMTD calculation for a single-pass shell, and a crossed programme needs a multi-pass arrangement or a different configuration. The sizing holds for the stated terminal temperatures and a single-pass arrangement; a changed temperature programme is outside the worked scope.

points: Setting: biodiesel production from waste cooking oil with an immobilised lipase catalyst
Enzyme loading 6 % by mass of oil; methanol to oil molar ratio 4.5
Reaction time 24 hours at 313 kelvin
Oil conversion 94 %
Conversion after 8 reuse cycles 88 %
definitions: lipase = an enzyme that catalyses the reaction of oils with methanol to form biodiesel
immobilised = fixed on a solid support for recovery and reuse
oil conversion = the fraction of the charged oil converted to biodiesel
methanol to oil molar ratio = the amount of methanol divided by the amount of oil, each in moles
prose: Waste cooking oil carries a disposal cost and a variable composition, and a production route that tolerates the variability has direct value for small biodiesel plants. This study tests an immobilised lipase route, lipase being an enzyme that catalyses the reaction of oils with methanol to form biodiesel, and immobilised meaning fixed on a solid support for recovery and reuse. Enzyme loading was 6 % by mass of oil, and the methanol to oil molar ratio, the amount of methanol divided by the amount of oil with each in moles, was 4.5. Batches ran for 24 hours at 313 kelvin with stepwise methanol addition. Oil conversion, the fraction of the charged oil converted to biodiesel, reached 94 %. Conversion after 8 reuse cycles of the same catalyst charge was 88 %. Glycerol separated cleanly from the product under the stated settling procedure, and no soap formation was detected in the product at the stated feed water content. The immobilised catalyst holds conversion across reuse cycles with a shallow decline, and stepwise methanol addition carries the tolerance to the variable feed. The route suits small plants that value catalyst reuse over batch speed.

points: Setting: lithium recovery from a salt lake brine with a selective sorbent
Feed lithium concentration 240 milligrams per litre; magnesium to lithium ratio in the feed 18
Sorbent capacity 14 milligrams of lithium per gram of sorbent
Extraction efficiency 91 % of the lithium in the feed
Product magnesium to lithium ratio 1.6
Capacity loss 3 % over 30 loading cycles
definitions: sorbent = a solid that takes up a target ion from solution on its surface and releases the ion into a second solution
extraction efficiency = the amount of lithium recovered in the product stream divided by the amount of lithium in the feed
magnesium to lithium ratio = the mass of magnesium divided by the mass of lithium in the same stream
prose: Salt lake brines hold lithium at low concentration beside a large excess of magnesium, and a separation that rejects magnesium decides the cost of lithium recovery from the resource. This study measures a selective sorbent route, a sorbent being a solid that takes up a target ion from solution on its surface and releases the ion into a second solution. Feed lithium concentration was 240 milligrams per litre, and the magnesium to lithium ratio in the feed, the mass of magnesium divided by the mass of lithium in the same stream, was 18. Packed columns of the sorbent were loaded with brine, washed, and stripped in a repeating cycle. Sorbent capacity reached 14 milligrams of lithium per gram of sorbent. Extraction efficiency, the amount of lithium recovered in the product stream divided by the amount of lithium in the feed, was 91 %. The product magnesium to lithium ratio was 1.6. Capacity loss over 30 loading cycles was 3 %. The sorbent separates lithium from magnesium by a wide margin in a single loading stage, and the shallow capacity loss across cycles keeps the separation open to continuous operation. Brine treatment with a selective sorbent is a workable front end for lithium recovery at the stated feed composition.

points: A single microchannel of width 600 micrometres delivers 0.8 kilograms of product per day
Target plant throughput 400 kilograms per day
A numbering-up array of 500 channels reaches the target throughput at the stated per-channel rate
Pressure drop per channel 85 kilopascals at the stated flow
Residence time 45 seconds in a single channel
Flow distribution across a large parallel array is unmeasured, and maldistribution across channels is the open question
definitions: microchannel = a channel with a width below one millimetre, where surface forces and short diffusion paths govern the flow
numbering-up = replication of identical channels in parallel to raise throughput, in place of enlargement of a single channel
residence time = the average time a fluid element spends inside the channel
limits: The study covers numbering-up of identical channels; enlargement of a single channel is outside the study scope
prose: Microchannel reactors carry fast and exothermic reactions with a control that stirred vessels cannot match, and a microchannel, a channel with a width below one millimetre where surface forces and short diffusion paths govern the flow, gives that control at laboratory scale. A single channel of width 600 micrometres delivers 0.8 kilograms of product per day. Plant demand sits far above the single-channel rate, and the target plant throughput in this study is 400 kilograms per day. Numbering-up, the replication of identical channels in parallel to raise throughput in place of enlargement of a single channel, is the established route from the laboratory device to plant rates. An array of 500 channels reaches the target throughput at the stated per-channel rate. Established work covers reaction performance inside a single channel and inside small arrays. Flow distribution across a large parallel array is unmeasured, and maldistribution across channels is the open question: a channel starved of flow runs long, a channel flooded with flow runs short, and the product record of the array carries both faults. Pressure drop per channel is 85 kilopascals at the stated flow, and residence time, the average time a fluid element spends inside the channel, is 45 seconds. This study measures flow distribution across a full array with tracer injection at the shared inlet and sampling at grouped outlets, and the study covers numbering-up of identical channels; enlargement of a single channel is outside the study scope.

points: Solvent loss by degradation 0.42 kilograms per tonne of carbon dioxide captured
Heat-stable salt content 3.1 % of the solvent inventory at the end of the campaign
Pilot campaign length 2000 hours on a coal flue gas slipstream
Oxygen partial pressure in the treated gas 21 kilopascals
Degradation rates to be measured at 313 kelvin, 333 kelvin, and 353 kelvin
The split of solvent degradation between the oxidative route and the thermal route in operating solvent is unmeasured

degradation rate = the loss of active amine per unit time under stated conditions
flue gas slipstream = a side draw from the main flue gas flow, treated in the pilot unit

Established work reports degradation rates for fresh solvent in bench apparatus under a single route at a time, oxidative or thermal. This study measures the degradation rate, the loss of active amine per unit time under stated conditions, at 313 kelvin, 333 kelvin, and 353 kelvin in solvent drawn from the pilot loop, with the oxidative route isolated by oxygen-free duplicates. The study covers one amine solvent on a coal flue gas slipstream; natural gas flue gas is outside the study scope.

points: Rotational rheometer with a concentric cylinder geometry and a measuring gap of 1.0 millimetres
Sample volume 19 millilitres per measurement
Measurement temperature 323 kelvin, held by a circulating bath
Pre-shear period 60 seconds and rest period 300 seconds before each measurement
Shear rate sweep from 0.1 to 1000 reciprocal seconds
Replicates 4 per sample; repeatability 2.4 % as a coefficient of variation
definitions: rheometry = the measurement of the flow properties of a fluid under controlled shear
shear rate = the velocity gradient imposed on the sample across the measuring gap
coefficient of variation = the standard deviation of repeated measurements divided by their mean, a measure of spread
yield stress = the stress below which the sample does not flow
limits: The procedure covers the stated temperature and shear rate range; samples with settled solids are outside the procedure scope
prose: Rheometry, the measurement of the flow properties of a fluid under controlled shear, followed a fixed procedure for every drilling fluid sample. A rotational rheometer with a concentric cylinder geometry and a measuring gap of 1.0 millimetres held the sample. Sample volume was 19 millilitres per measurement, loaded with a syringe to keep air out of the gap. Measurement temperature was 323 kelvin, held by a circulating bath, and the sample rested in the geometry until the temperature reading settled before any shear was applied. Warning: an exposed sample edge dries during long runs and stiffens the record, and a solvent trap covered the sample for every measurement in the sweep. Each measurement opened with a pre-shear period of 60 seconds at the top rate, and a rest period of 300 seconds followed before the sweep began. The shear rate sweep, the velocity gradient imposed on the sample across the measuring gap, ran from 0.1 to 1000 reciprocal seconds in ascending steps, with the matching descending sweep recorded straight after. Replicates numbered 4 per sample, each from a fresh loading. Repeatability was 2.4 % as a coefficient of variation, the coefficient of variation being the standard deviation of repeated measurements divided by their mean, a measure of spread. A reference oil of certified viscosity verified the instrument at the start of each session, and a session opened only after the reference reading fell inside its certified band. Yield stress, the stress below which the sample does not flow, and the flow curve came from a Herschel and Bulkley fit to the descending sweep. The procedure covers the stated temperature and shear rate range; samples with settled solids are outside the procedure scope.

points: Pilot fluidised bed combustor rated at 150 kilowatts thermal
Operating record 640 hours on the stated coal
Bed temperature 1123 kelvin held across the record
Combustion efficiency 98.6 %
Sulphur capture 89 % at a calcium to sulphur molar ratio of 2.1
Sorbent utilisation 42 %
Nitrogen oxide emissions 180 milligrams per cubic metre of dry flue gas
definitions: fluidised bed = a bed of solid particles suspended in a rising gas stream, mixing as a fluid
combustion efficiency = the fraction of the fuel carbon that leaves the combustor as carbon dioxide
sulphur capture = the fraction of the fuel sulphur retained in the bed solids
sorbent utilisation = the fraction of the charged calcium that has reacted with sulphur
limits: One coal type was tested; high-ash coals are outside the tested scope
The unit is pilot scale; heat transfer surfaces of a full-scale unit are outside the tested scope
prose: The pilot campaign supports one claim at the tested scope: a fluidised bed, a bed of solid particles suspended in a rising gas stream and mixing as a fluid, burns the stated coal cleanly at pilot scale with in-bed sulphur capture. The combustor is rated at 150 kilowatts thermal, and the operating record covers 640 hours on the stated coal. Bed temperature held at 1123 kelvin across the record. Combustion efficiency, the fraction of the fuel carbon that leaves the combustor as carbon dioxide, was 98.6 %. Sulphur capture, the fraction of the fuel sulphur retained in the bed solids, was 89 % at a calcium to sulphur molar ratio of 2.1. Sorbent utilisation, the fraction of the charged calcium that has reacted with sulphur, was 42 %. Nitrogen oxide emissions were 180 milligrams per cubic metre of dry flue gas. prose: Gas absorption into a liquid film, and drying of a wet solid, both rest on transport through a thin stagnant layer at the interface. The molar flux J, the amount of a species crossing a unit area per unit time, states the transport rate through the film. The Fick relation gives the flux as the negative product of the diffusion coefficient and the concentration gradient across the film: J equals minus D multiplied by the change in c over the change in x, where D is the diffusion coefficient of the species in the film medium, c is the concentration of the species in the film, and x is the distance across the film, measured from the interface. The negative sign carries the direction of transport: the flux runs from high concentration toward low concentration, against the direction in which c rises. The diffusion coefficient in the relation is the value at a film temperature of 298 kelvin for the stated species and medium pair, and the coefficient belongs to the pair rather than to the species alone. A boundary case stands next to the relation. For films thinner than 1 millimetre, the concentration profile stays close to linear, and the gradient in the relation can be read as the concentration difference across the film divided by the film thickness. At a uniform concentration the gradient vanishes, and the flux vanishes with the gradient. The relation in the stated form holds for a dilute species in a stagnant film; a concentrated mixture carries a bulk flow term that the stated form omits.

Alkalinity was measured by titration of the water sample with standard acid to a fixed endpoint, with the result stated as milligrams per litre of calcium carbonate equivalent. Alkalinity is the acid-neutralising capacity of a water sample. The titrant acid concentration was 0.1 moles per litre, standardised against dried sodium carbonate before the sample set was run. Sample volume was 50 millilitres, delivered by pipette into a conical flask with a measured addition of indicator solution. The titration endpoint was a pH of 4.5, read on the bench pH meter rather than by the indicator colour alone; the endpoint is the pH at which the titration is stopped and the titre is read, and the titre is the volume of titrant delivered from the burette at the endpoint. Acid was added slowly near the endpoint with the flask swirled continuously. Where the endpoint is passed before the reading is taken, the titration is discarded and the sample is titrated again: an overshot endpoint inflates the titre, and no correction recovers the discarded run.

Each sample received 3 replicate titrations, and the reported alkalinity is the mean of the replicates. A blank titration on the dilution water preceded each sample set, and the blank titre was subtracted from every sample titre before the calculation. Alkalinity was computed from the corrected titre, the acid concentration, and the sample volume, with the equivalent mass of calcium carbonate as the conversion factor. A standard check solution of 250 milligrams per litre gave a recovery of 98 percent across the study, and a failed check stopped sample work until the acid was restandardised. The method covers samples titrated promptly after collection, and stored samples with biological activity stand outside the procedure.

prose:
Algal biofuel production grows algae in open ponds and converts the harvested biomass to fuel, and the economics of the route turn on the productivity a pond sustains outdoors. Reported areal productivity (biomass produced per unit pond area per day, in grams per square metre per day) spans 12 to 25 g per square metre per day across published pond studies. The spread across studies is wide, and the studies differ in climate, pond depth, mixing, and harvest practice. The pilot pond has an area of 0.5 hectares. Pond operating depth is 0.3 metres. Harvest concentration in the pilot pond reaches 0.8 g per litre.

Established pond operation controls temperature by depth, controls acidity by carbon dioxide addition, and harvests by flocculation (the clumping of suspended cells into aggregates that settle) and settling. The controlled variables are the cheap ones. Productivity under variable light is the uncontrolled case: light at the pond surface changes with cloud cover on a timescale of minutes, algae in the mixed pond move between surface light and depth shade, and the productivity response to that fluctuating light field is a missing piece of knowledge. Steady-light laboratory measurements give a photosynthesis response that the pond never sees, and pond models built on the steady response mispredict the outdoor record in both directions.

The study measures the productivity response of the pond culture to fluctuating light. The pilot pond carries continuous light logging at the surface and at depth, and a laboratory rig exposes the same culture to light programmes replayed from the pond record, with productivity measured on both routes across the same periods.

points: The scan ran from 10 to 80 degrees.
Step size was 0.02 degrees, with a counting time of 2 seconds per step.
Tube voltage was 40 kilovolts, and tube current was 30 milliamperes.
The sample carried 10 % by mass of corundum as an internal standard.
Phase fractions from the refinement carry an estimated uncertainty of 1.5 % by mass.
definitions: Rietveld refinement = a least-squares fit of a calculated diffraction pattern to the measured pattern, returning phase fractions
internal standard = a phase of known amount added to the sample, against which the amorphous content is measured
phase fraction = the mass fraction of one crystalline phase in the sample
limits: The method quantifies crystalline phases in the stated scan range; amorphous content enters through the internal standard, and a phase below the detection level of the refinement carries no reported fraction.
prose:
Phase quantification by X-ray diffraction used a powder diffractometer with a copper anode tube and a position-sensitive detector. Samples were ground to a fine powder, mixed with the internal standard, and back-loaded into the sample holder to limit preferred orientation of the crystallites. The scan ran from 10 to 80 degrees. Step size was 0.02 degrees, with a counting time of 2 seconds per step. Tube voltage was 40 kilovolts, and tube current was 30 milliamperes. The sample carried 10 % by mass of corundum as an internal standard (a phase of known amount added to the sample, against which the amorphous content is measured). The holder rotated during the scan, and the rotation averaged the crystallite orientations presented to the beam. A repeat scan of the same preparation checked the stability of the pattern before the refinement began.

Phase fractions (the mass fraction of one crystalline phase in the sample) were obtained by Rietveld refinement (a least-squares fit of a calculated diffraction pattern to the measured pattern, returning phase fractions). The refinement fitted the scale factor of each crystalline phase, the lattice parameters of each phase, a background function, and a peak-shape function, in that order, with the instrument profile fixed from a standard scan. The internal standard anchors the amorphous content: the refinement returns crystalline fractions normalised to the crystalline total, and the known standard addition rescales the fractions to the whole sample, with the remainder reported as amorphous content. Phase fractions from the refinement carry an estimated uncertainty of 1.5 % by mass, estimated from repeat preparations of a reference mixture. The method quantifies crystalline phases in the stated scan range; amorphous content enters through the internal standard, and a phase below the detection level of the refinement carries no reported fraction.

definitions: optical probe = a probe in which oxygen quenches the luminescence of a sensing dye, and the quenching gives the oxygen concentration
span value = the reading assigned to air-saturated water at the calibration temperature
Winkler titration = a chemical titration that fixes the oxygen in the sample and titrates the released iodine

prose:
Dissolved oxygen was measured with an optical probe (a probe in which oxygen quenches the luminescence of a sensing dye, and the quenching gives the oxygen concentration). Calibration used two points, a zero point and a span point, in that order. Zero calibration used a sodium sulfite solution at 20 g per litre, with the probe held in the solution until the reading was stable at zero. The span point used air-saturated water, prepared by bubbling air through water at constant temperature until successive readings agreed. Air-saturated water at 25 degrees Celsius gave the span value (the reading assigned to air-saturated water at the calibration temperature) of 8.3 mg per litre. Barometric pressure at calibration was 101 kilopascals, and the probe applied the pressure correction internally from a manual entry.

Temperature compensation used the temperature sensor in the probe cap, and the calibration record carries the temperature of both calibration solutions. Readings were taken with the probe moving slowly through the sample, and a reading taken in still water was discarded. Acceptance allows a drift of 0.2 mg per litre over 24 hours, tested by returning the probe to air-saturated water at the end of the field day. Calibration was confirmed by Winkler titration (a chemical titration that fixes the oxygen in the sample and titrates the released iodine) on a split sample, and the probe and titration values agreed within the acceptance drift. The calibration record for each probe carries the date, the operator, the solution batch, and the two calibration readings, and the record travels with the probe data file. Probes failing the drift test were recalibrated, and a second failure removed the sensing cap from service. Calibration holds for the stated temperature and pressure route, and a probe used outside the drift acceptance carries no valid calibration.

prose:
The retrofit replaced a gas boiler with an industrial heat pump lifting waste heat from the process cooling circuit to the site heating circuit. Heat delivered by the retrofit heat pump was 850 kilowatts. Electricity drawn was 250 kilowatts, and the coefficient of performance (the ratio of heat delivered to electricity drawn) was 3.4. The source temperature was 35 degrees Celsius, and the delivery temperature was 72 degrees Celsius. Operation was metered over 11 months. Avoided gas use corresponds to 1280 tonnes of carbon dioxide per year. Payback on the installed cost was 4.6 years at the metered performance.

The principal result is the coefficient of performance at the tested lift (the temperature difference between the delivery temperature and the source temperature): the heat pump delivered the site heat load at the stated source and delivery temperatures across the metered period, through the seasonal swing of both circuits. Performance at part load was weaker than performance near full load, and the metered average carries the part-load hours of the shoulder seasons. Two scope conditions bound the claim. The delivery temperature was held at the stated value by the heating circuit control, and a higher delivery temperature lowers the coefficient of performance by raising the lift. The source was process waste heat at the stated temperature, and a colder source in a production shutdown lies outside the metered record. Refrigerant leakage across the period was below the detection of the charge record, and long-term degradation of the compressor lies beyond the metered period. Within the tested scope, the retrofit stands as a measured replacement for the boiler duty the heat pump took over, at the metered coefficient of performance.

points: Boundary case: at Q of 1, the logarithm is 0 and E equals the standard cell potential.
R is 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin, and F is 96485 coulombs per mole.
The standard cell potential E° is 1.10 V for the zinc and copper cell.
At a temperature T of 298 kelvin, R times T divided by F is 0.0257 V.
The electron number n for the zinc and copper reaction is 2.
At a reaction quotient Q of 0.05, the natural logarithm of Q is -3.00.
The correction term is 0.0386 V.
The cell potential E at that quotient is 1.14 V.
definitions: E = cell potential, in volts
E° = standard cell potential, the cell potential at the standard composition, in volts
R = gas constant
T = absolute temperature, in kelvin
Q = reaction quotient, the ratio of product activities to reactant activities
n = number of electrons transferred in the cell reaction
F = Faraday constant, the charge of one mole of electrons
limits: The equation holds for a cell reaction with the electrodes at equilibrium, at the stated temperature; activity coefficients are carried inside the activities in Q.
prose:
Cell potential changes with the composition of the cell, and the Nernst equation carries that change in a single relation. The cell potential E (the voltage of an electrochemical cell under a stated composition, in volts) is the central quantity. The Nernst equation gives E as the standard cell potential E° minus the product of R, T, and the natural logarithm of Q, divided by the product of n and F. In the equation, E° is the standard cell potential (the cell potential at the standard composition), R is the gas constant, T is the absolute temperature, Q is the reaction quotient (the ratio of product activities to reactant activities), n is the number of electrons transferred in the cell reaction, and F is the Faraday constant (the charge of one mole of electrons). At the boundary case of Q of 1, the logarithm is 0 and E equals the standard cell potential.

R is 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin, and F is 96485 coulombs per mole. The standard cell potential E° is 1.10 V for the zinc and copper cell. At a temperature T of 298 kelvin, R times T divided by F is 0.0257 V. The electron number n for the zinc and copper reaction is 2. At a reaction quotient Q of 0.05, the natural logarithm of Q is -3.00. The correction term is 0.0386 V. The cell potential E at that quotient is 1.14 V. The potential stands above the standard potential because the quotient sits below the boundary value: products are scarcer than the standard composition, and the cell reaction has further to run before the quotient reaches the equilibrium value. The equation holds for a cell reaction with the electrodes at equilibrium, at the stated temperature, and activity coefficients are carried inside the activities in Q.

Superficial velocity covered 0.05 to 0.20 metres per second; pressure gradient reached 1.8 kilopascals per metre at the lowest velocity and 12.6 kilopascals per metre at the highest velocity.
At an intermediate velocity the measured gradient was 5.4 kilopascals per metre against a predicted gradient of 5.1 kilopascals per metre.
Ergun correlation predicted 11.4 kilopascals per metre at the highest velocity; the measured gradient exceeded the predicted gradient by 10.5 percent, with the excess growing with velocity.

Wall channeling near the column wall is the interpretation offered for an excess that grows with velocity.
definitions: superficial velocity = volumetric flow rate divided by the empty-column cross-sectional area
pressure gradient = pressure drop per unit bed length
spread of a reported gradient = standard deviation of the repeat measurements at a fixed velocity
predicted pressure gradient = model output of the Ergun correlation computed from the measured void fraction and the superficial velocity
limits: Claims are bound to the tested velocity range and to beds of the same packing.
prose:
Pressure drop across the packed bed rose with superficial velocity over the full range tested. The bed held glass spheres with a particle diameter of 3 millimetres and a void fraction of 0.42, and air passed upward through a bed height of 1.2 metres. Superficial velocity, the volumetric flow rate divided by the empty-column cross-sectional area, covered 0.05 to 0.20 metres per second. The pressure gradient, the pressure drop per unit bed length, reached 1.8 kilopascals per metre at the lowest velocity and 12.6 kilopascals per metre at the highest velocity. Each reported gradient is the mean of 18 repeat measurements at a fixed velocity, and the spread of a reported gradient is the standard deviation of those repeats, 0.9 kilopascals per metre at the highest velocity. Pressure transducers at the bed inlet and the bed outlet recorded the pressure drop at each velocity after the reading settled.

The Ergun correlation, applied at the same void fraction and particle diameter, gave a predicted pressure gradient of 11.4 kilopascals per metre at the highest velocity. The predicted pressure gradient is a model output, computed from the measured void fraction and the superficial velocity, and the predicted pressure gradient carries no measurement spread. The measured gradient exceeded the predicted gradient by 10.5 percent at the highest velocity, and the excess grew with velocity over the range tested. At an intermediate velocity the measured gradient was 5.4 kilopascals per metre, and the predicted gradient at the same velocity was 5.1 kilopascals per metre. Flow channeling near the column wall is consistent with an excess that grows with velocity, because a wall channel carries a rising share of the flow as velocity rises. At the lowest velocity the measured and predicted gradients agreed within the spread of the repeats. The agreement at low velocity and the excess at high velocity bound the correlation for this bed to the tested velocity range and to beds of the same packing.

points: Worked example goal: conversion of a reactant in a batch reactor with first-order kinetics after a stated holding time at a stated temperature; prerequisites are a batch material balance and the exponential function.
Rate constant 0.045 per minute at 75 degrees Celsius; initial reactant concentration 0.80 moles per litre; reactor volume 2 litres; holding time 60 minutes; constant temperature and mixed contents.

Exponent is the rate constant multiplied by the holding time and evaluates to 2.7; residual fraction is the exponential of the negative exponent and evaluates to 0.067; conversion is the complement of the residual fraction and is 93.3 percent.
Check with the half-life: the exponent reaches 0.693 at 15.4 minutes, and the holding time is near four half-lives.
Warning: a rate constant from a table at a different temperature is a common error; the temperature attached to the rate constant is checked before any arithmetic.
definitions: rate constant = proportionality factor between the rate and the reactant concentration for a first-order reaction
residual fraction = fraction of reactant remaining at the holding time
conversion = fraction of reactant consumed
half-life = time at which the exponent reaches the stated check value
limits: Outcome stated for the stated temperature and the stated holding time only.
prose:
This tutorial computes the conversion of a reactant in a batch reactor with first-order kinetics, and the worked example ends with a checked conversion value that you can reproduce with a hand calculator. The prerequisites are a material balance on a batch vessel and the exponential function. Work through the example with the stated values first, and repeat the same three quantities with a new holding time as practice. The goal is the conversion after a stated holding time at a stated temperature.

The reaction is first-order in the reactant: the rate is the product of the rate constant and the reactant concentration. The rate constant, the proportionality factor in that rate expression, is 0.045 per minute at 75 degrees Celsius. The initial reactant concentration is 0.80 moles per litre, and the reactor volume is 2 litres. The holding time is 60 minutes. The temperature stays constant during the holding time, the vessel contents are mixed, and a single concentration describes the vessel at each instant. A common error is a rate constant taken from a table at a different temperature: check the temperature attached to the rate constant before any arithmetic.

Carry the calculation in three quantities. Keep the units attached to every quantity in the written work, and state the conversion as a percentage at the end. The exponent is the product of the rate constant and the holding time, and the exponent evaluates to 2.7. The residual fraction, the fraction of reactant remaining at the holding time, is the exponential of the negative exponent, and the residual fraction evaluates to 0.067. The conversion, the fraction of reactant consumed, is the complement of the residual fraction, and the conversion is 93.3 percent. Check the result before use. The half-life, the time at which the exponent reaches 0.693, is 15.4 minutes, and a holding time near four half-lives leaves a residual fraction near the value computed above. The conversion states the outcome for the stated temperature and the stated holding time, and a longer holding time at the same temperature raises the conversion toward complete consumption of the reactant.

points: Setting: flue gas from gas-fired power stations carries carbon dioxide at a mole fraction near 0.15; membrane separation is a capture route without a solvent regeneration step.
Aim: a thin-film composite membrane giving a permeate enriched in carbon dioxide at a low stage cut, with the retentate composition near the feed composition.
Method: membranes cast with a selective layer thickness of 35 micrometres; 6 membrane samples tested with a mixed feed at the stated mole fraction.
Principal result: carbon dioxide flux 0.42 moles per square metre per hour; selectivity 48; permeate carbon dioxide mole fraction 0.89.
Durability: the membrane held the stated flux over 500 hours of continuous testing.
Implication: membrane capture at the stated selectivity and the stated flux is a retrofit candidate for gas-fired stations where a solvent plant has no steam supply to spare.
definitions: thin-film composite membrane = selective polymer layer on a porous support
selectivity = ratio of the carbon dioxide permeance to the nitrogen permeance
prose: Flue gas from gas-fired power stations carries carbon dioxide at a mole fraction near 0.15, and membrane separation offers a capture route without a solvent regeneration step. This study reports a thin-film composite membrane, a selective polymer layer on a porous support, built for that separation, and the study aim is a permeate enriched in carbon dioxide at a stage cut low enough to leave the retentate composition near the feed composition. Membranes were cast with a selective layer thickness of 35 micrometres, and 6 membrane samples were tested with a mixed feed at the stated mole fraction. The carbon dioxide flux through the membrane was 0.42 moles per square metre per hour, and the selectivity, the ratio of the carbon dioxide permeance to the nitrogen permeance, was 48. The permeate mole fraction of carbon dioxide reached 0.89. The selectivity at the measured flux places the permeate composition within the range required for a downstream compression step, and the membrane held the stated flux over 500 hours of continuous testing. Membrane capture at the stated selectivity and the stated flux is a candidate for retrofit on gas-fired stations where a solvent plant has no steam supply to spare.

Cooling water on the tube side at 1.4 kilograms per second; hot stream entered the shell side at 85 degrees Celsius; cold stream entered at 20 degrees Celsius.

Readings taken every 7 days at matched flow rates; a reading accepted after port temperatures held steady over a full sampling interval; thermocouples calibrated against a reference thermometer before the run and at the end of the run.

Clean overall coefficient 1450 watts per square metre per kelvin, measured in the first days after a chemical clean; fouled overall coefficient 980 watts per square metre per kelvin at the end of the run.
Fouling resistance at the end of the run was 0.00033 square metres kelvin per watt.

A second exchanger of the same design, cleaned on the same schedule and instrumented with the same procedure, gave the independent route for the clean baseline.
definitions: overall coefficient = duty divided by the product of the heat transfer area and the log mean temperature difference
fouling resistance = difference between the reciprocal of the fouled overall coefficient and the reciprocal of the clean overall coefficient; a computed quantity with no direct sensor
limits: Readings are comparable only at matched flow rates.
prose:
Fouling was tracked on a shell-and-tube exchanger in cooling water service over a 90 day run. The exchanger held 24 tubes of length 2.4 metres, and the heat transfer area was 1.9 square metres. Cooling water flowed on the tube side at 1.4 kilograms per second, and the hot stream entered the shell side at 85 degrees Celsius with the cold stream entering at 20 degrees Celsius. Thermocouples at the four ports were calibrated against a reference thermometer before the run, and the calibration was repeated at the end of the run.

Readings were taken every 7 days at matched flow rates, and a reading was accepted after the port temperatures held steady over a full sampling interval. The duty came from the tube-side flow rate and the tube-side temperature rise, and the overall coefficient came from the duty and the log mean temperature difference. The clean overall coefficient, measured in the first days after a chemical clean, was 1450 watts per square metre per kelvin. The fouled overall coefficient at the end of the run was 980 watts per square metre per kelvin. The fouling resistance is the difference between the reciprocal of the fouled overall coefficient and the reciprocal of the clean overall coefficient, and the fouling resistance is a computed quantity with no direct sensor. The fouling resistance at the end of the run was 0.00033 square metres kelvin per watt. Each temperature reading is the mean of 3 repeat readings, and the spread of a temperature reading is the standard deviation of the repeats, within 0.2 kelvin on every occasion. A second exchanger of the same design, cleaned on the same schedule and instrumented with the same procedure, gave the independent route for the clean baseline.

Mass fraction of polymer above 300 kilograms per mole was 9 percent of the total polymer mass.
Monomer conversion at sampling was 87 percent; reactor temperature held at 70 degrees Celsius.

weight-average molar mass = average of the molar mass weighted by the mass in each fraction
dispersity = ratio of the weight-average molar mass to the number-average molar mass

prose:
Polymerization in a stirred batch reactor gave a polymer with a broad molar mass distribution at high conversion. The distribution came from gel permeation chromatography on dissolved samples, with molar masses read against a calibration built from narrow standards. The number-average molar mass, the total mass of polymer divided by the total number of chains and expressed per mole of chains, was 48 kilograms per mole. The weight-average molar mass, the average weighted by the mass in each fraction, was 121 kilograms per mole. The dispersity, the ratio of the weight-average molar mass to the number-average molar mass, was 2.52. A high molar mass tail carried the dispersity: the mass fraction of polymer above 300 kilograms per mole was 9 percent of the total polymer mass. Monomer conversion at sampling was 87 percent, and the reactor temperature was held at 70 degrees Celsius over the run.

The predicted number-average molar mass is a model output from the monomer-to-initiator ratio at full conversion, scaled by the measured conversion, and the predicted number-average molar mass was 52 kilograms per mole. The measured number-average molar mass fell below the predicted value by 7.7 percent. Chain transfer to solvent adds chains beyond the count set by the initiator, and added chains lower the number-average molar mass at a fixed monomer mass. The dispersity was measured on samples from 5 batches run at the stated conversion and the stated temperature, and the spread of the dispersity is the standard deviation of the batch values, 0.08. Within the conversion range tested, and at the stated temperature, the dispersity held near the stated value across the batches, and no batch showed a dispersity outside the spread of the batch values. The high molar mass tail grew with conversion inside each batch, and the tail accounts for the weight-average molar mass standing far above the number-average molar mass.

points: Setting: the works treats a flow of 40 megalitres per day; influent ammonia nitrogen concentration 42 milligrams per litre; effluent consent limit 2 milligrams per litre.
Required removal is 95.2 percent of the influent ammonia nitrogen.

Established knowledge: nitrification is established practice for the removal; aeration lanes with long solids retention times are the standard vessel; the design solids retention time at this works is 9 days.
Hard case: winter mixed liquor temperature 12 degrees Celsius, where the nitrifier growth rate is the lowest of the year and the margin to washout narrows.

Gap: the nitrifier fraction of the mixed liquor at full scale is not measured at this works, and design values come from laboratory cultures grown apart from the works liquor; growth rates from cultures may misstate the rate in the works liquor.

Aim and method preview: measure the nitrification rate and the nitrifier fraction in the works liquor across the seasons and compare the measured rate against the design value at the winter temperature; respirometry on liquor samples is the measurement route, with 4 sampling campaigns across the seasonal range.
definitions: nitrification = oxidation of ammonia to nitrate by nitrifying bacteria
solids retention time = mean residence time of the sludge solids in the works
limits: Claims are scoped to this works, with the winter temperature as the hard case.
prose: Municipal wastewater carries ammonia nitrogen from domestic sewage, and discharge consents set a limit on the ammonia nitrogen in the treated effluent. The works in this study treats a flow of 40 megalitres per day, with an influent ammonia nitrogen concentration of 42 milligrams per litre against a consent limit of 2 milligrams per litre in the effluent. Removal of 95.2 percent of the influent ammonia nitrogen is required across the works. Nitrification, the oxidation of ammonia to nitrate by nitrifying bacteria, is established practice for that removal, and aeration lanes with long solids retention times are the standard vessel. A solids retention time of 9 days is the design value at this works. Winter operation sets the hard case: at a mixed liquor temperature of 12 degrees Celsius the nitrifying bacteria grow at the lowest rate of the year, and the margin between the design solids retention time and washout narrows. The nitrifier fraction of the mixed liquor at full scale is not measured at this works, and design values come from laboratory cultures grown apart from the works liquor. Growth rates from laboratory cultures may misstate the rate in the works liquor, because the liquor carries inhibitors and a mixed population that a culture lacks. This study measures the nitrification rate and the nitrifier fraction in the works liquor across the seasons, and the study compares the measured rate against the design value at the winter temperature. Respirometry on liquor samples, with sludge age and temperature recorded at each sampling, is the measurement route, and 4 sampling campaigns cover the seasonal range.

Reynolds number for the worked values is 99800; the ratio of pipe length to pipe diameter is 300.
Blasius correlation gives the friction factor as 0.316 multiplied by the Reynolds number raised to the power of minus one quarter; the friction factor evaluates to 0.0178.
Dynamic pressure is 1996 pascals; the pressure drop evaluates to 10.7 kilopascals.
Interpretation: the pressure drop grows with the square of the mean velocity at a fixed friction factor.
definitions: Δp = pressure drop, the fall in pressure along a straight pipe section, in pascals
f = friction factor, dimensionless
L = pipe length, in metres
D = pipe diameter, in metres
ρ = fluid density, in kilograms per cubic metre
v = mean velocity, in metres per second
μ = dynamic viscosity, in pascal seconds

prose:
The pressure drop for pipe flow, Δp, is the fall in pressure along a straight pipe section, stated in pascals, and the Darcy–Weisbach relation states that pressure drop from the friction factor and the flow conditions. The relation gives the pressure drop as the product of the friction factor, the ratio of pipe length to pipe diameter, and the dynamic pressure, where the dynamic pressure is one half of the fluid density multiplied by the square of the mean velocity, where f is the friction factor (dimensionless), L is the pipe length (in metres), D is the pipe diameter (in metres), ρ is the fluid density (in kilograms per cubic metre), and v is the mean velocity (in metres per second). The friction factor depends on the Reynolds number, the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in the flow, defined as the product of the fluid density, the mean velocity, and the pipe diameter, divided by the dynamic viscosity μ (in pascal seconds).

For a pipe of length 15 metres and diameter 0.05 metres carrying water of density 998 kilograms per cubic metre at a mean velocity of 2.0 metres per second, with a dynamic viscosity of 0.001 pascal seconds, the Reynolds number is 99800 and the ratio of pipe length to pipe diameter is 300. For smooth pipe the friction factor comes from the Blasius correlation, which states the friction factor as 0.316 multiplied by the Reynolds number raised to the power of minus one quarter, and the friction factor evaluates to 0.0178. The Blasius correlation holds for Reynolds numbers below 100000 and for smooth pipe walls, and the worked Reynolds number sits below that boundary. The dynamic pressure is 1996 pascals, and the pressure drop evaluates to 10.7 kilopascals. The pressure drop grows with the square of the mean velocity at a fixed friction factor, and a velocity change is the strongest lever on the pressure drop.

severity = the operating intensity of the reformer, set in this work by reactor inlet temperature

prose:
Reformate octane performance was measured on a pilot catalytic reformer operated at two severity levels. The catalyst was a platinum-on-alumina formulation held in a fixed bed, and the bed had completed a standard regeneration before the campaign opened. The feed was a straight-run naphtha (research octane number 64.0), and sampling at each condition began after line-out at the separator outlet. Pressure (1.4 megapascals), liquid hourly space velocity (2.8 per hour) and hydrogen-to-hydrocarbon molar ratio (5.2) held constant across the runs. Reactor inlet temperature set the severity level (490 degrees Celsius at low severity, 515 degrees Celsius at high severity).
Product research octane number reached 98.2 at high severity (91.4 at low severity), and the octane gain tracked the aromatics content of the reformate (68.4 % by mass at high severity, 57.9 % by mass at low severity). Aromatisation reactions carry the gain: dehydrogenation of naphthenes and dehydrocyclisation of paraffins raise the aromatics fraction, and the aromatics fraction carries the knock resistance of the blend. Liquid yield moved against octane (82.6 % by mass at high severity, 87.3 % by mass at low severity), and hydrocracking at the higher temperature priced the octane gain in liquid product. Benzene in the high-severity reformate was 0.8 % by volume, inside a specification limit of 1.0 % by volume. Octane values are means of triplicate determinations, and the standard deviation of a determination was 0.6 octane units. The high-severity product held octane across the stability run, with a decline of 1.8 octane units over 400 hours on stream. For feeds with a sulphur content below 10 milligrams per kilogram, the high-severity condition delivered a reformate at the higher octane level inside the benzene specification (Fig. 1). The trade-off between octane and liquid yield sets the operating choice for a commercial unit, and the choice turns on the price spread between high-octane blendstock and liquid product volume in the market served.

points: Wetland: horizontal subsurface-flow bed, surface area 850 square metres, gravel bed depth 0.6 metres.
Hydraulic loading rate 0.12 metres per day; nominal hydraulic retention time 5.5 days.
Influent total phosphorus averaged 6.8 milligrams per litre; effluent total phosphorus averaged 1.9 milligrams per litre; removal 72 %.
Effluent values are means over 14 monthly campaigns; standard deviation of the monthly effluent means 0.4 milligrams per litre.
Winter performance: effluent total phosphorus 2.6 milligrams per litre; removal 62 %.
Harvested above-ground biomass accounted for 18 % of the phosphorus load removed over the year.
definitions: total phosphorus = the phosphorus concentration of an unfiltered sample after digestion, stated as elemental phosphorus
hydraulic retention time = the water volume of the bed divided by the volumetric flow rate through the bed
hydraulic loading rate = the volumetric inflow divided by the surface area of the bed
limits: The removal claim holds for influent total phosphorus at or above 4.0 milligrams per litre.
figures: Fig. 1: monthly influent and effluent total phosphorus concentrations across the sampling year
prose:
Phosphorus removal was measured in a horizontal subsurface-flow constructed wetland treating settled municipal wastewater. The bed was planted with common reed over a gravel matrix, and flow passed below the gravel surface along the full length of the bed. The wetland had a surface area of 850 square metres and a gravel bed depth of 0.6 metres, and the hydraulic loading rate was 0.12 metres per day (nominal hydraulic retention time 5.5 days). Sampling points stood at the inlet distribution chamber and at the outlet collection chamber, and total phosphorus was measured by colorimetry after digestion of unfiltered samples.
Influent total phosphorus averaged 6.8 milligrams per litre, and effluent total phosphorus averaged 1.9 milligrams per litre (removal 72 % across the wetland). Effluent values are means over 14 monthly campaigns, and the standard deviation of the monthly effluent means was 0.4 milligrams per litre. Removal weakened in winter. Effluent total phosphorus rose to 2.6 milligrams per litre in the winter campaigns, and removal fell to 62 %. The seasonal pattern followed plant dormancy and falling water temperature: plant uptake slowed, microbial activity in the rhizosphere slowed, and sorption onto the gravel carried a larger share of a smaller removal. Harvested above-ground biomass accounted for 18 % of the phosphorus load removed over the year, and the harvested fraction left the system in the cut material. The balance of the removed load stayed in the bed, held by sorption and accretion in the gravel matrix. For influent total phosphorus at or above 4.0 milligrams per litre, the wetland held the stated removal across all seasons sampled (Fig. 1). A second bed operated in parallel received the same wastewater, and the two beds agreed on the seasonal pattern while differing in the depth of the winter decline. Design values taken from the campaign belong to the loading range of the bed as built, and a bed loaded beyond that range carries a shorter contact time per unit of flow.

points: The extract was frozen at minus 40 degrees Celsius and held until the full charge reached shelf temperature.
Primary drying ran at a chamber pressure of 12 pascals for 38 hours.

Residual moisture after primary drying alone was 4.6 % by mass; after secondary drying the residual moisture was 1.8 % by mass.
Residual moisture values are means across 6 vials per batch; the standard deviation was 0.3 percentage points.
After storage for 90 days at 25 degrees Celsius in sealed vials, residual moisture rose to 2.4 % by mass.
Reconstitution time in warm water was 45 seconds.
definitions: residual moisture = the mass of water remaining in the dried product divided by the dry solids mass, stated as a percentage
primary drying = the stage in which ice leaves the frozen product by sublimation under vacuum
secondary drying = the stage in which bound water leaves the dried matrix at raised shelf temperature

figures: Fig. 1: residual moisture by drying stage for the programme with secondary drying and the programme without
prose:
Residual moisture was measured for a coffee extract freeze-dried under a programme with a secondary drying stage and a programme that ended after primary drying. The extract was frozen at minus 40 degrees Celsius and held until the full charge reached shelf temperature. Primary drying ran at a chamber pressure of 12 pascals for 38 hours, with the sublimation front moving from the vial top toward the base as the dried layer thickened. Secondary drying raised the shelf to 30 degrees Celsius for 8 hours. Residual moisture was measured by Karl Fischer titration, a coulometric method that reacts water in the sample with a reagent and counts the charge consumed.
Residual moisture after primary drying alone was 4.6 % by mass, and after secondary drying the residual moisture was 1.8 % by mass (Fig. 1). Residual moisture values are means across 6 vials per batch, and the standard deviation was 0.3 percentage points. The gap between the two programmes sits in the bound water of the dried matrix: primary drying removes ice by sublimation and leaves adsorbed water in place, and the raised shelf temperature of secondary drying supplies the energy that desorbs the bound fraction. Cake structure held across both programmes, with no collapse, no shrinkage from the fill line and no melt-back at the vial base. After storage for 90 days at 25 degrees Celsius in sealed vials, residual moisture rose to 2.4 % by mass, and the rise records moisture ingress through the stopper rather than a change in the cake. Reconstitution time in warm water was 45 seconds for the secondary-dried product, and the reconstituted extract carried no undissolved solids. For a fill depth of 10 millimetres in the vial, the programme with secondary drying delivered the lower residual moisture at the cost of the added shelf time.

points: Current density was run at 450 amperes per square metre and at 600 amperes per square metre.

Deposits were harvested on a 24 hour cycle.

current density = the cell current divided by the cathode area
electrowinning = the electrodeposition of a metal from a leach electrolyte in an electrolytic cell

figures: Fig. 1: current efficiency and cell voltage against current density
prose:
Current efficiency was measured in pilot zinc electrowinning cells run at two current density levels with a synthetic electrolyte. Cathodes were aluminium blanks and anodes were a lead-silver alloy, and deposits were stripped, washed, dried and weighed at the end of each cycle. Current density was run at 450 amperes per square metre and at 600 amperes per square metre. The electrolyte carried zinc at 55 grams per litre and sulphuric acid at 160 grams per litre, at 38 degrees Celsius.
Current efficiency reached 91.2 % at the lower current density and 84.6 % at the higher current density (Fig. 1). Cell voltage was 3.4 volts at the lower current density and 3.8 volts at the higher current density. Energy consumption at the lower current density was 3.06 kilowatt-hours per kilogram of zinc deposited. The efficiency loss at the higher current density sits in hydrogen evolution at the cathode: a larger share of the charge reduces protons rather than zinc ions, and the deposit at the higher current density grew rougher, with nodules at the blank edges where local current density peaks. A cobalt addition trial gave a current efficiency of 78.3 % with cobalt at 0.4 milligrams per litre, and cobalt acts on the same route, catalysing hydrogen evolution on the deposit surface. Deposits were harvested on a 24 hour cycle. Current efficiency values are means over 5 cells, and the standard deviation was 1.1 percentage points. For electrolyte with iron below 2 milligrams per litre, the lower current density delivered the higher efficiency at the lower energy consumption. The operating choice between the two current density levels trades efficiency against tankhouse throughput, and a plant running at the higher level passes more metal per cell per day while paying for the gain in energy and in deposit quality. Electrolyte purification carries the cobalt result: cobalt control upstream of the cells protects the efficiency recorded at either level.

points: Factors and levels: temperature at 160 degrees Celsius (low) and 180 degrees Celsius (high); catalyst loading at 1 % by mass (low) and 3 % by mass (high).

Main effect of catalyst loading: 8.5 percentage points of yield.
Interaction effect: 2.5 percentage points of yield.

definitions: factorial design = an experiment in which every level of each factor is run in combination with every level of each other factor
main effect = the change in the mean response when a factor moves from its low level to its high level, averaged over the levels of the other factors
interaction = the change in the effect of one factor between the levels of another factor, stated at half the difference by the convention of a two-level design
centre point = a run at the midpoint of every factor range, used to test for curvature
