prose:
This tutorial builds a two-level factorial design for a reactor study and reads the factor effects from the completed runs. You end with three effect estimates and a curvature check, and you need a response measured at every corner of the design before the arithmetic starts. The response here is yield, and the factors are temperature and catalyst loading.
Set the levels first. Temperature runs at 160 degrees Celsius (low) and 180 degrees Celsius (high), and catalyst loading runs at 1 % by mass (low) and 3 % by mass (high). Run every combination, and randomise the run order where the apparatus allows the order to vary: run order confounds drift with factor effects when the runs follow the table order. The completed yields, in percent, were: low temperature with low catalyst 42; high temperature with low catalyst 55; low temperature with high catalyst 48; high temperature with high catalyst 66.
Average the yields at each level of a factor to read the main effect of that factor. The main effect of temperature was 15.5 percentage points of yield: raising temperature raised yield across both catalyst loadings. The main effect of catalyst loading was 8.5 percentage points of yield. Compare the temperature effect at each catalyst loading to read the interaction. The interaction effect was 2.5 percentage points of yield, small against the two main effects, and the small interaction marks a response that the two factors move near-additively across the tested ranges. Check the design with a centre point before extending the ranges. The mean of the corner yields was 52.75 %, and the centre-point yield was 53 %; the centre point sits on the corner mean, and curvature inside the ranges is negligible at the precision of the runs. The effect estimates hold inside the factor ranges tested; a two-level design does not map curvature away from the centre point, and a search for an optimum beyond the corners needs a design that maps the curvature.

prose:
This tutorial sizes a packed humidification tower that raises the humidity of an air stream by contact with recirculated water. You finish with a tower diameter, a packed height and a gas-side pressure drop. You need the gas flow, the inlet state of the air and the target outlet humidity before the sizing starts.
Start from the water balance. The dry air flow to the tower is 2.5 kilograms of dry air per second. The inlet humidity ratio is 0.008 kilograms of water per kilogram of dry air, and the target outlet humidity ratio is 0.020 kilograms per kilogram. The evaporation rate required by the water balance is 0.030 kilograms per second, and the make-up water line must supply the evaporation rate plus the blowdown stream. The inlet dry-bulb temperature is 40 degrees Celsius, and the outlet dry-bulb temperature is 27 degrees Celsius at the design approach to saturation; evaporation cools the air toward the wet-bulb temperature as the humidity ratio climbs. Check the evaporation rate against the humidity change before sizing the packing: the rate follows from the dry air flow and the humidity ratio difference alone, and an error here propagates into every later quantity.
Set the diameter from the gas velocity. Keep the superficial velocity below the flooding velocity of the packing at the design liquid rate; flooding fills the packing with liquid and the pressure drop climbs without bound. The flooding-checked gas velocity gives a packing cross-section of 3.1 square metres and a tower diameter of 2.0 metres. Set the packed height from the transfer duty. The number of transfer units for the duty is 2.4, the height of a transfer unit is 0.9 metres, and the packed height is 2.16 metres. Close with the pressure drop. The packing pressure drop is 180 pascals per metre of packed height, and the total gas-side pressure drop is 389 pascals; the fan duty follows from the total. The sizing holds for adiabatic operation with negligible heat loss through the tower wall.

points: The body: a steel sphere of diameter 25 millimetres.

The cooling calculation carries a logarithm term of 7 in the temperature ratio; cooling time to the target temperature: 253 seconds.
definitions: Biot number = the ratio of internal conduction resistance to surface convection resistance in a body, calculated as the heat transfer coefficient multiplied by the characteristic length and divided by the thermal conductivity
characteristic length = the volume of a body divided by its surface area
time constant = the product of density, characteristic length and specific heat capacity divided by the heat transfer coefficient, for a body cooled under the lumped capacitance model

prose:
This tutorial estimates the cooling time of a hot steel sphere in a quench bath with the lumped capacitance model, and checks the model before trusting the estimate. You finish with a cooling time and with the validity check that licenses the time. You need the sphere size, the steel properties, the surface heat transfer coefficient and the two bath temperatures at the start.
Take the body and the properties first. The body is a steel sphere of diameter 25 millimetres. The steel properties are: density 7800 kilograms per cubic metre; specific heat capacity 480 joules per kilogram kelvin; thermal conductivity 45 watts per metre kelvin. The heat transfer coefficient at the sphere surface is 120 watts per square metre kelvin. The characteristic length of the sphere is 4.17 millimetres, that is 0.00417 metres; a sphere carries the largest volume-to-area ratio of the common shapes, and the characteristic length records that geometry in a single length.
Run the validity check before the cooling arithmetic. The Biot number of the sphere is 0.011, against the lumped-model criterion of 0.1. The Biot number sits an order of magnitude inside the criterion, and the temperature inside the sphere stays near-uniform during the quench: conduction inside the steel redistributes heat far faster than convection removes heat at the surface. A Biot number near the criterion withdraws that licence, and a body at the boundary needs a distributed conduction solution in place of the lumped model.
Carry the temperatures and the time constant into the cooling calculation. The initial sphere temperature is 300 degrees Celsius, the quench fluid stands at 20 degrees Celsius, and the target temperature is 60 degrees Celsius. The time constant of the sphere is 130 seconds. The cooling calculation carries a logarithm term of 7 in the temperature ratio, and the cooling time to the target temperature is 253 seconds. Read the result against the time constant: the sphere needs about two time constants to close most of the temperature gap, and the long tail of the exponential sets the last part of the wait. The cooling time holds while the heat transfer coefficient stays at the design value; boiling at the surface changes the coefficient and the time constant with it.

points: Peak external quantum efficiency: 21.4 %.
Brightness reached 8500 candelas per square metre at a current density of 10 milliamperes per square centimetre.
Operating time to half the initial luminance: 320 hours at an initial luminance of 1000 candelas per square metre, against 85 hours for the control device.
Emission peak at 520 nanometres, with a full width at half maximum of 24 nanometres.
Efficiency values are means over 18 devices; the standard deviation was 1.3 percentage points.

turn-on voltage = the applied voltage at which a device reaches a set reference luminance
prose: Light-emitting diodes based on metal halide perovskite films are efficient emitters, and device lifetime under continuous operation has limited the material class in display applications. A mixed-cation perovskite emitter with a polymer interlayer at the hole-injection contact was fabricated and tested against a control device built without the interlayer. The interlayer device emitted in the green, with an emission peak at 520 nanometres and a full width at half maximum of 24 nanometres, and a turn-on voltage of 2.3 volts. Peak external quantum efficiency reached 21.4 %, and brightness reached 8500 candelas per square metre at a current density of 10 milliamperes per square centimetre. Efficiency values are means over 18 devices, and the standard deviation was 1.3 percentage points. The operating time to half the initial luminance was 320 hours at an initial luminance of 1000 candelas per square metre, against 85 hours for the control device. The interlayer suppresses ion migration at the contact, and the lifetime gain at equal efficiency assigns the dominant degradation route to the contact rather than the emitter bulk. Perovskite diodes with contact-side stabilisation meet the efficiency and lifetime levels that display backlight development requires, and the fabrication route uses solution coating throughout, a route that transfers to large-area substrates.

prose: Solid oxide fuel cells convert hydrogen and air directly into electricity at high temperature, and cell resistance sets the power available from a given cell area. An anode-supported cell with a thin electrolyte and a cobalt-free cathode was fabricated and tested against a baseline cell with a conventional cathode. The electrolyte thickness was 8 micrometres, and the operating temperature was 750 degrees Celsius. The test cell outperformed the baseline at every point of the current-voltage characteristic. Peak power density reached 1.12 watts per square centimetre (0.74 watts per square centimetre for the baseline cell), with an open-circuit voltage of 1.08 volts and an area-specific resistance of 0.18 ohm square centimetres at the operating temperature. Power values are means over 6 cells, and the standard deviation of peak power density was 0.05 watts per square centimetre. Peak power fell by 3.8 % over 500 hours of operation. The resistance gain assigns the improvement to the cathode: the cobalt-free composition kept the polarisation resistance of the conventional cathode while the thin electrolyte cut the ohmic share. Anode-supported cells of this construction deliver stack-level power density at the tested temperature on a cathode free of cobalt.

Heat delivered to customers annually: 310 gigawatt-hours.

The oldest pipe sections have been in service for 38 years.
The logging campaign covers 26 substations over 12 months.

uncertainty = the half-width of the interval within which the modelled loss for a network section is expected to lie

prose:
District heating moves heat from a central plant to buildings through buried pipe, and the heat lost in transit is paid for at the plant and delivered nowhere. The network studied here carries 42 kilometres of buried supply and return pipe, delivers 310 gigawatt-hours of heat to customers annually, and runs at design temperatures of 95 degrees Celsius supply and 55 degrees Celsius return. The estimated distribution loss for the network is 14 % of the heat generated. Losses reported for comparable networks span 8 % to 18 % of heat generated, and the spread between networks of similar age and load reflects insulation state, burial depth, groundwater contact and return temperature discipline.
The network total is known from plant and customer metering. The split of the total among network sections is not known: no section of the network carries the flow and temperature logging that a section balance requires, and the oldest pipe sections have been in service for 38 years with insulation state recorded only at excavation. A replacement programme priced by section needs the split, ranked by loss per unit length, before capital follows the ranking. This study measures the split. Flow and temperature logging at 26 substations over 12 months feeds a section-by-section heat balance, calibrated against the metered network total. The loss model will report each section loss with an uncertainty of 2 percentage points, and sections will be ranked by loss per unit length with the uncertainty carried into the ranking. The loss split applies to the pipe stock as surveyed; a section replaced during the campaign leaves the model at replacement.

points: Sulphuric acid leaching in published laboratory studies recovers 92 % of the cobalt in black mass.
The published leaching conditions centre on an acid concentration of 2 moles per litre at 80 degrees Celsius.
Lithium recovery in the same published routes reaches 70 %.
The feed characterised in this study carries iron at 12 % by mass.
The leach test programme covers 5 feed grades.
Residence times in the leach tests extend to 4 hours.
Characterisation covers 3 industrial black mass samples.
definitions: black mass = the shredded and separated electrode material from spent lithium-ion batteries, carrying the cathode metals
leaching = the dissolution of target metals from a solid into a liquid phase
feed grade = the metal content class of a black mass batch, set by the battery chemistry of the source stream

prose:
Spent lithium-ion batteries return to recyclers as black mass, and leaching moves the cathode metals from the black mass into a liquor that refining can separate. Sulphuric acid leaching in published laboratory studies recovers 92 % of the cobalt in black mass, and lithium recovery in the same published routes reaches 70 %. The published leaching conditions centre on an acid concentration of 2 moles per litre at 80 degrees Celsius, with a reductant added to bring cobalt into solution. The published record rests on single-chemistry feeds prepared for the laboratory: sorted cells of one cathode type, milled to a controlled size, with the fluorine and iron burden of a mixed industrial stream absent.
Industrial black mass arrives mixed. Cathode chemistries blend in the shredder, current collector fragments ride with the electrode material, and the feed characterised in this study carries iron at 12 % by mass. Recovery of cobalt and lithium from a mixed feed at the published conditions is not recorded, and the acid consumption of the impurity load is unrecorded; the gap sits in the transfer from a sorted laboratory feed to the stream a plant receives. This study measures that transfer. Characterisation covers 3 industrial black mass samples, spanning the grade range of the receiving stream. The leach test programme covers 5 feed grades drawn from the characterised samples, and residence times in the leach tests extend to 4 hours. Metal recovery, acid consumption and residue composition close each test, and recovery is reported against the characterised feed grade of the sample leached. The programme addresses hydrometallurgical leaching only; pyrometallurgical pretreatment of the same feeds falls outside the study.

Temperature rise on combustion of the standard: 2.412 kelvin.
Fuse wire and acid formation corrections in the calibration totalled 61 joules.
Energy equivalent of the calorimeter: 10780 joules per kelvin.
The bomb was charged with oxygen at 3.0 megapascals.
Samples were dried at 105 degrees Celsius for 2 hours before pelleting.
The thermometer resolves 0.001 kelvin.
Calibration was repeated over 5 combustions; the standard deviation of the energy equivalent was 24 joules per kelvin.
Bomb temperature was recorded every 10 seconds through the firing and the after-period.
definitions: energy equivalent = the heat capacity of the calorimeter assembly, stated as the energy that raises the bomb and its contents by one kelvin
bomb calorimeter = a sealed constant-volume vessel in which a sample burns in oxygen and the released energy passes to the surrounding water jacket
after-period = the interval after combustion during which the temperature drift of the calorimeter is recorded for the cooling correction
limits: The calibration applies to the bomb, bucket and water charge as assembled; a change of water charge or bomb internals requires recalibration.
prose:
Energy of combustion was measured in a bomb calorimeter, a sealed constant-volume vessel in which the sample burns in oxygen and the released energy passes to the surrounding water jacket. Calibration preceded the sample programme and used benzoic acid as the standard. The calibration mass was 0.986 grams of benzoic acid, with a certified energy of combustion of 26434 joules per gram. The bomb was charged with oxygen at 3.0 megapascals, fired by a fuse wire, and the temperature rise on combustion of the standard was 2.412 kelvin. Bomb temperature was recorded every 10 seconds through the firing and the after-period, and the cooling correction came from the drift recorded in the after-period. Fuse wire and acid formation corrections in the calibration totalled 61 joules. The energy equivalent of the calorimeter was 10780 joules per kelvin. Calibration was repeated over 5 combustions, and the standard deviation of the energy equivalent was 24 joules per kelvin.
Samples were dried at 105 degrees Celsius for 2 hours before pelleting, and each pellet was weighed into the crucible immediately before the bomb closed. The thermometer resolves 0.001 kelvin, and the resolution sets the floor of the temperature-rise measurement against which the cooling correction is applied. Sample combustions followed the calibration sequence exactly: the same oxygen charge, the same water charge, the same firing circuit and the same correction set, with the energy of combustion of the sample calculated from the measured temperature rise and the energy equivalent of the calorimeter. The calibration applies to the bomb, bucket and water charge as assembled; a change of water charge or bomb internals requires recalibration before further samples are fired. Firing records for every combustion are retained with the sample record.

points: Plasma gas flow: 15 litres per minute of argon; auxiliary gas flow 0.9 litres per minute; nebuliser gas flow 0.7 litres per minute.
Radio-frequency power applied to the plasma: 1300 watts.
Calibration used 5 standard levels: 0.05, 0.10, 0.50, 1.00 and 5.00 milligrams per litre.
Internal standard: yttrium held at 2.00 milligrams per litre in every solution.
Digestion: sample mass 0.250 grams, acid volume 9 millilitres, final dilution to 50 millilitres.
Detection limit for cadmium: 0.003 milligrams per litre, set from 10 blank digestions.
Spike recovery: 97 % at a spike level of 0.20 milligrams per litre.
Rinse time between samples: 60 seconds.
Cadmium was measured at the 228.8 nanometre emission line.
definitions: ICP = inductively coupled plasma, the ionised argon discharge that atomises and excites the sample in the spectrometer
detection limit = the lowest concentration the method reports, set at three times the standard deviation of blank digestions
internal standard = an element held at a fixed concentration in every solution, used to correct signal drift during a run
limits: Concentrations above the highest calibration level were diluted and re-run; the calibration does not extend by extrapolation.
prose:
Element concentrations in digested samples were measured by inductively coupled plasma (ICP) optical emission spectrometry, in which a nebulised sample solution enters an argon plasma and element concentrations are read from the emission spectrum of the plasma. Digestion came first. Each sample was weighed at 0.250 grams into a digestion vessel, the acid volume was 9 millilitres, and the cooled digest was diluted to 50 millilitres. A blank digestion accompanied every batch, and the batch blank carried the full acid and vessel sequence with no sample.
Plasma conditions held constant across the programme. The plasma gas flow was 15 litres per minute of argon, the auxiliary gas flow was 0.9 litres per minute, and the nebuliser gas flow was 0.7 litres per minute. Radio-frequency power applied to the plasma was 1300 watts. Cadmium was measured at the 228.8 nanometre emission line, and every element was read at a line free of overlap from the matrix elements at the concentrations present. Calibration used 5 standard levels: 0.05, 0.10, 0.50, 1.00 and 5.00 milligrams per litre, prepared in the same acid matrix as the digests. Yttrium served as internal standard, held at 2.00 milligrams per litre in every solution; sample signals were ratioed to the yttrium signal before the calibration applied, and the ratio corrects nebuliser drift during a run. The detection limit for cadmium was 0.003 milligrams per litre, set from 10 blank digestions. Spike recovery was 97 % at a spike level of 0.20 milligrams per litre, and a failed spike recovery stopped the batch for re-digestion. The rinse time between samples was 60 seconds. Concentrations above the highest calibration level were diluted and re-run; the calibration does not extend by extrapolation.

points: The tested cure cycle ramped at 2 degrees Celsius per minute to a dwell at 180 degrees Celsius, held for 120 minutes.
Glass transition temperature of the cured laminate: 196 degrees Celsius.
Interlaminar shear strength reached 78 megapascals, against 71 megapascals for the manufacturer cycle.
Void content was 0.8 % by volume, against 1.9 % by volume for the manufacturer cycle.
Flexural strength was 1240 megapascals, with a standard deviation of 45 megapascals across 8 coupons.
Panel thickness in the trial: 4 millimetres.
Total cycle time fell by 35 % against the manufacturer cycle.
definitions: glass transition temperature = the temperature at which the cured resin passes from a glassy to a rubbery state, measured here by differential scanning calorimetry
interlaminar shear strength = the shear strength between plies of a laminate, measured in a short-beam bending test
void content = the volume fraction of enclosed gas in the cured laminate
limits: The claim covers panels at the tested thickness; sections above 12 millimetres were not tested.
One prepreg batch was tested; batch-to-batch variation and humidity ageing stand outside the trial.
prose:
The trial supports a shortened cure cycle for the tested panel construction, at the tested thickness and on the tested prepreg batch. The tested cycle ramped at 2 degrees Celsius per minute to a dwell at 180 degrees Celsius, held for 120 minutes, and total cycle time fell by 35 % against the manufacturer cycle. Laminates from the shortened cycle carried a glass transition temperature of 196 degrees Celsius. Interlaminar shear strength reached 78 megapascals (71 megapascals for the manufacturer cycle), and void content was 0.8 % by volume (1.9 % by volume for the manufacturer cycle). Flexural strength was 1240 megapascals, with a standard deviation of 45 megapascals across 8 coupons. Panel thickness in the trial was 4 millimetres.
The shortened cycle gains time in the ramp and holds the dwell at the manufacturer temperature, and the property set records no penalty for the gain: the slower ramp lets volatiles leave the lay-up before the resin gels, and the void content records the effect. The claim covers panels at the tested thickness; sections above 12 millimetres were not tested, and thick sections cure under an exotherm that the thin-panel trial does not reproduce. One prepreg batch was tested; batch-to-batch variation and humidity ageing stand outside the trial, and a production release needs both before the cycle replaces the manufacturer schedule in service parts. The autoclave programme as tested is ready for a repeat trial on a second prepreg batch, with the same coupon plan and the same acceptance values carried over from this trial.

standard deviation = the spread of the replicate breakthrough times about their mean, stated in the caption with the replication count
saturation time = the elapsed time at which the outlet concentration reaches the inlet concentration
figures: Fig. 1: breakthrough curve for the fixed bed under the stated feed conditions
prose: Fig. 1 | Breakthrough curve for a fixed bed of activated carbon (adsorbent charge 250 grams) fed with a vapour stream at a feed concentration of 400 parts per million by volume and a feed flow rate of 2.0 litres per minute, at a bed temperature of 25 degrees Celsius and a pressure of 101 kilopascals. points: Wall material thermal conductivity: 1.4 watts per metre kelvin.
Wall area: 12 square metres.
Wall thickness: 0.25 metres.
Face temperatures: 20 degrees Celsius at the hot face and 5 degrees Celsius at the cold face.
Temperature difference across the wall: 15 kelvin.
Temperature gradient through the wall: 60 kelvin per metre in magnitude.
Heat transfer rate from the evaluation: 1008 watts.
definitions: q = the heat transfer rate through the wall, in watts
k = the thermal conductivity of the wall material, in watts per metre kelvin
A = the wall area normal to the heat flow, in square metres
T = the temperature in the wall, in degrees Celsius
x = the distance through the wall, in metres, measured from the hot face
limits: The relation holds for steady one-dimensional conduction with constant thermal conductivity; at a zero temperature gradient the heat transfer rate is zero.
prose:
Heat conduction through a plane wall at steady state carries a heat transfer rate set by the material, the geometry and the temperature field in the wall. The heat transfer rate q, stated in watts, is the quantity the relation predicts: q is the energy crossing the wall per unit time. For the wall treated here, q equals the negative product of the thermal conductivity k, the wall area A and the temperature gradient dT/dx, the rate of change of temperature T with distance x through the wall. In the relation, k is the thermal conductivity of the wall material in watts per metre kelvin, A is the wall area normal to the heat flow in square metres, T is the temperature in degrees Celsius, and x is the distance through the wall in metres, measured from the hot face. The relation holds for steady, one-dimensional conduction with a thermal conductivity that does not vary with temperature, and a zero temperature gradient gives a zero heat transfer rate; a wall with a uniform temperature conducts no heat under the relation, at either face temperature.
The wall evaluated here has a thermal conductivity of 1.4 watts per metre kelvin, an area of 12 square metres and a thickness of 0.25 metres, with face temperatures of 20 degrees Celsius at the hot face and 5 degrees Celsius at the cold face. The temperature difference across the wall is 15 kelvin, and the temperature gradient through the wall is 60 kelvin per metre in magnitude. The heat transfer rate from the evaluation is 1008 watts, directed from the hot face toward the cold face. The negative sign in the relation carries that direction: temperature falls along the direction of the heat flow, and the gradient term records the fall.

points: Particle diameter fell from 212 nanometres at a surfactant concentration of 0.4 grams per litre to 118 nanometres at 1.6 grams per litre, with an intermediate value of 156 nanometres at 0.8 grams per litre; polymerizations at 70 degrees Celsius.
Each diameter is the mean of 3 batches at the stated concentration.
Polydispersity index fell from 0.21 at the lowest surfactant concentration to 0.08 at the highest concentration, with 0.12 at the intermediate concentration.
Monomer conversion reached 96 percent at 180 minutes in every run; solids content of each latex was 20 percent by mass.
definitions: particle diameter = volume-weighted mean diameter measured by dynamic light scattering
dynamic light scattering = sizing method that infers particle size from the fluctuation of scattered light intensity
polydispersity index = dimensionless width of the particle size distribution from the same measurement
surfactant concentration = mass of surfactant per litre of the aqueous phase
limits: The trend holds within the surfactant range tested and in the single reactor geometry used.
figures: Fig. 1: particle diameter against surfactant concentration for styrene emulsion polymerization
prose: Fig. 1 shows particle diameter against surfactant concentration for styrene emulsion polymerization at 70 degrees Celsius. The particle diameter, the volume-weighted mean diameter measured by dynamic light scattering, fell from 212 nanometres at a surfactant concentration of 0.4 grams per litre to 118 nanometres at 1.6 grams per litre, with an intermediate value of 156 nanometres at 0.8 grams per litre. Dynamic light scattering infers particle size from the fluctuation of scattered light intensity, and the instrument software converts the intensity-weighted distribution to the volume-weighted mean under a spherical particle assumption. Stirrer speed, monomer feed profile, and initiator dose were held constant across the surfactant concentrations, and the surfactant concentration is the single varied quantity in the design. The fall in particle diameter across the surfactant range tested in the single reactor geometry reflects a larger number of micelles available for particle nucleation at the higher surfactant concentrations, and the diameter at each concentration is the mean of 3 batches. The polydispersity index, the dimensionless width of the size distribution from the same measurement, fell from 0.21 at the lowest surfactant concentration to 0.08 at the highest concentration, with 0.12 at the intermediate concentration. A distribution narrows as nucleation ends earlier in the reaction, and the index values carry the same ordering as the diameter values. Monomer conversion reached 96 percent at 180 minutes in every run, and the solids content of each latex was 20 percent by mass. Conversion at a fixed solids content holds the polymer mass constant across the surfactant concentrations, and a smaller diameter at a fixed polymer mass corresponds to a larger particle number. Particle size control by surfactant dose in the tested range moves diameter and distribution width in the same direction, and the latex at the highest surfactant concentration carries the smallest diameter and the narrowest distribution of the concentrations tested.

points: Burner retrofit on 6 gas turbines at a coastal power station; emissions record over 8000 operating hours.
Nitrogen oxide concentration fell from 38 milligrams per cubic metre of dry gas to 17 milligrams per cubic metre, a reduction of 55 percent.
The reduction held across the load range from 50 percent to 100 percent of rated output.
Carbon monoxide concentration at the lowest load tested was 14 milligrams per cubic metre.
Plant efficiency was 56.2 percent before the retrofit and 55.9 percent after the retrofit.
definitions: nitrogen oxide concentration = sum of nitric oxide and nitrogen dioxide in the flue gas, expressed as nitrogen dioxide equivalent per cubic metre of dry gas
dry low emission burner = premixed burner that lowers peak flame temperature
load = electrical output stated as a percentage of rated output
carbon monoxide concentration = mass of carbon monoxide per cubic metre of dry gas
limits: The record covers a single coastal station burning natural gas; sulphur-bearing fuels sit outside the tested scope.
prose: Nitrogen oxide emissions from 6 gas turbines fell after a dry low emission burner retrofit, over 8000 operating hours at a coastal power station. A dry low emission burner is a premixed burner that lowers peak flame temperature, and the retrofit replaced the diffusion burners on each turbine with premixed burners and retuned the fuel staging schedule during commissioning. Emissions were recorded by the continuous monitoring system on each turbine stack, and the reported concentrations are hourly averages corrected to the reference oxygen condition of the station permit. The nitrogen oxide concentration, the sum of nitric oxide and nitrogen dioxide expressed as nitrogen dioxide equivalent, fell from 38 milligrams per cubic metre of dry gas to 17 milligrams per cubic metre at the coastal site, a reduction of 55 percent, and the reduction held across the load range from 50 percent to 100 percent of rated output, load being electrical output stated as a percentage of rated output. Lower peak flame temperature suppresses thermal nitrogen oxide formation, and the flat emissions profile across the load range shows the staging schedule holding flame temperature near the design point at part load. The carbon monoxide concentration, the mass of carbon monoxide per cubic metre of dry gas, was 14 milligrams per cubic metre at the lowest load tested, and a carbon monoxide rise at low load is the known cost of leaner combustion at part load. Plant efficiency was 56.2 percent before the retrofit and 55.9 percent after the retrofit, and the efficiency change sits within the variation of the station heat rate record. Nitrogen oxide emissions at the station now sit below the permit limit for the load range of normal dispatch. The emissions record and the efficiency record rest on the same operating hours, and burner condition at the next overhaul stands as the maintenance watch item for the station.

points: Feed ore gold grade 2.1 grams per tonne; pulp density 40 percent solids by mass; solution pH 10.5; thiosulfate concentration 0.15 moles per litre.
Gold extraction reached 61.2 percent at 8 hours and 84.6 percent at 24 hours for the oxide ore tested.
Residual gold in the leach residue was 0.32 grams per tonne.
Thiosulfate consumption was 18.4 kilograms per tonne of ore over the leach.
definitions: gold extraction = fraction of the gold in the feed ore dissolved into solution, stated as a percentage
pulp density = mass of dry solids divided by the total mass of the pulp, stated as a percentage
thiosulfate leaching = dissolution of gold into an aqueous thiosulfate solution with a copper catalyst and an ammonia stabiliser
residual gold = gold remaining in the solid residue after leaching, per tonne of dry residue
limits: The extraction values hold for the oxide ore tested; sulphide ores and carbonaceous ores sit outside the tested scope.
prose: Gold extraction by thiosulfate leaching reached 84.6 percent at 24 hours for the oxide ore tested, against a feed ore gold grade of 2.1 grams per tonne. Gold extraction is the fraction of the gold in the feed ore dissolved into solution, stated as a percentage, and thiosulfate leaching is the dissolution of gold into an aqueous thiosulfate solution with a copper catalyst and an ammonia stabiliser. The leach ran at a pulp density of 40 percent solids by mass, pulp density being the mass of dry solids divided by the total mass of the pulp, at a solution pH of 10.5 and a thiosulfate concentration of 0.15 moles per litre. Extraction reached 61.2 percent at 8 hours, and the extraction curve flattens between the two sampling times as the accessible gold surface is depleted. Residual gold in the leach residue was 0.32 grams per tonne, residual gold being the gold remaining in the solid residue after leaching, and the residual grade matches the extraction figure against the feed grade within the rounding of the two assays. Thiosulfate consumption was 18.4 kilograms per tonne of ore over the leach, and consumption is the main operating cost term in the reagent balance. The extraction level at the stated consumption places thiosulfate leaching in the range of cyanidation for the oxide ore tested, with a reagent cost carried by consumption rather than by gold loss to the residue. A longer leach raises extraction along the flattened part of the curve, and the gain in dissolved gold per added hour falls as the residue grade approaches the residual level. Ore texture sets the accessible gold surface in the tested scope, and a finer grind enters the comparison only as a separate leach condition with a separate consumption record. Assay of the residue by a second laboratory confirmed the residual grade, and the confirmation route is the residue assay rather than the solution assay.

topic: Laplace transform solution of an ordinary differential equation
points: Worked example: a stirred tank whose contents temperature rise y, in kelvin, follows the balance: rate of change of y with time plus 2 multiplied by y equals 8, with y starting at zero.
Transformed balance: the factor s plus 2 multiplies the transform of y, and the right side is 8 divided by s.
Partial fractions: 8 divided by the product of s and s plus 2 separates into 4 divided by s minus 4 divided by s plus 2.
Solution: y equals 4 minus 4 multiplied by e raised to the power minus 2t; the steady temperature rise is 4 kelvin.
Check value: at t equal to 1 second, y equals 3.46 kelvin.
Check by substitution: the derivative of the solution is 8 multiplied by e raised to the power minus 2t, and the derivative plus 2 multiplied by y returns 8 at every time.
definitions: Laplace transform = integral transform that converts a function of time into a function of the complex frequency variable s
y = temperature rise of the tank contents above the inlet temperature, in kelvin
t = time, in seconds
s = complex frequency variable, in reciprocal seconds
steady temperature rise = value the temperature rise approaches as time grows without bound
limits: The balance holds while the tank volume, the flow rate, and the heat capacity of the contents stay constant.
prose: The goal is the temperature response of a stirred tank to a step change in heater power, obtained with the Laplace transform, and the outcome is a closed-form temperature history that a reader can evaluate at any time. The Laplace transform is an integral transform that converts a function of time into a function of the complex frequency variable s. The worked example takes a stirred tank whose contents temperature rise y, in kelvin, follows the balance in which the rate of change of y with time plus 2 multiplied by y equals 8, with y starting at zero, and the balance holds while the tank volume, the flow rate, and the heat capacity of the contents stay constant. Transformation of the balance gives the factor s plus 2 multiplying the transform of y, with the right side as 8 divided by s, where t is time in seconds and s is the complex frequency variable in reciprocal seconds. Partial fraction separation writes 8 divided by the product of s and s plus 2 as 4 divided by s minus 4 divided by s plus 2, and inversion of each term gives the solution y equals 4 minus 4 multiplied by e raised to the power minus 2t. The steady temperature rise, the value the temperature rise approaches as time grows without bound, is 4 kelvin. At t equal to 1 second the solution gives y equal to 3.46 kelvin, and the value sits below the steady rise by the amount the exponential term retains at that time. Substitution checks the solution: the derivative of the solution is 8 multiplied by e raised to the power minus 2t, and the derivative plus 2 multiplied by y returns 8 at every time, and the returned value is the right side of the original balance. A warning stands at the transform step: the initial condition enters the transform of the derivative, and a dropped initial condition shifts every later term of the solution.

points: Worked example inputs: hot water enters the tower at 42 degrees Celsius, cold water leaves at 32 degrees Celsius, and the entering air wet-bulb temperature is 24 degrees Celsius.
Range: the hot water temperature minus the cold water temperature gives 10 kelvin.
Approach: the cold water temperature minus the wet-bulb temperature gives 8 kelvin.
Duty: a circulation rate of 450 kilograms per second and a specific heat capacity of 4.18 kilojoules per kilogram per kelvin over the range give a duty of 18.8 megawatts.
Effectiveness: the range divided by the sum of the range and the approach gives 0.56.
definitions: range = fall in water temperature across the tower, in kelvin
approach = difference between the cold water temperature and the entering air wet-bulb temperature, in kelvin
wet-bulb temperature = lowest temperature air reaches by evaporative cooling at constant pressure
duty = rate of heat removal from the circulating water, in megawatts
effectiveness = range divided by the sum of the range and the approach, dimensionless
limits: The calculation treats the specific heat capacity of water as constant across the tower temperature interval.
prose: The goal is a cooling tower duty and an approach value from three measured temperatures and a circulation rate, and the outcome is a duty in megawatts with an approach that a reader can check against the wet-bulb limit. The worked example takes hot water entering the tower at 42 degrees Celsius, cold water leaving at 32 degrees Celsius, and an entering air wet-bulb temperature of 24 degrees Celsius. The wet-bulb temperature is the lowest temperature air reaches by evaporative cooling at constant pressure, and the wet-bulb temperature sets the floor for the cold water temperature. The range, the fall in water temperature across the tower, is the hot water temperature minus the cold water temperature and gives 10 kelvin. The approach, the difference between the cold water temperature and the entering air wet-bulb temperature, gives 8 kelvin, and a small approach carries a larger tower for the same duty. The duty, the rate of heat removal from the circulating water, follows from a circulation rate of 450 kilograms per second and a specific heat capacity of 4.18 kilojoules per kilogram per kelvin over the range, and the duty is 18.8 megawatts, with the specific heat capacity treated as constant across the tower temperature interval. The effectiveness, the range divided by the sum of the range and the approach, is 0.56, and the effectiveness states the achieved range as a fraction of the largest range the entering air permits. A checkpoint stands at the approach step: a negative approach is impossible for a tower in service, and a negative value in a calculation signals a transposed temperature or a wet-bulb reading taken downstream of the fill. The result shows a tower removing the stated duty with an approach in the range of normal industrial practice, and a design that demands a smaller approach buys the reduction with fill volume and fan power. A tower selected for a smaller approach carries more fill and a larger fan, and the trade stands in the design record beside the duty.

points: Worked example inputs: an orifice meter reads a differential pressure of 25 kilopascals with a standard uncertainty of 0.5 kilopascals, a relative uncertainty of 2 percent.
Flow rate from the meter is 3.2 kilograms per second; flow varies with the square root of the differential pressure, and the sensitivity coefficient for the pressure term is 0.5.
Pressure contribution to the relative uncertainty of flow: 1 percent.
Discharge coefficient carries a relative standard uncertainty of 0.8 percent; fluid density carries a relative standard uncertainty of 0.4 percent.
Combined relative standard uncertainty of flow: 1.3 percent; absolute standard uncertainty of flow: 0.043 kilograms per second.
Limiting check: with the pressure term removed, the combined value falls to 0.9 percent.
definitions: orifice meter = flow meter that infers flow rate from the pressure fall across a plate with a central hole
standard uncertainty = uncertainty of a measurement stated as a standard deviation
sensitivity coefficient = factor that converts the relative uncertainty of an input into the relative uncertainty of the result
combined standard uncertainty = root-sum-of-squares combination of the contribution of each input, stated for the result
discharge coefficient = factor that corrects the ideal orifice equation for friction and contraction of the jet
limits: The combination treats the three input uncertainties as independent; a shared calibration source for two inputs breaks the treatment.
prose: The goal is a flow rate with a defensible uncertainty, obtained by propagating the uncertainty of each input through the orifice meter equation, and the outcome is a combined standard uncertainty stated beside the flow rate. An orifice meter is a flow meter that infers flow rate from the pressure fall across a plate with a central hole. The worked example takes a differential pressure of 25 kilopascals with a standard uncertainty of 0.5 kilopascals, a standard uncertainty being an uncertainty stated as a standard deviation, and the relative uncertainty of the pressure reading is 2 percent. The meter gives a flow rate of 3.2 kilograms per second. Flow varies with the square root of the differential pressure, and the sensitivity coefficient for the pressure term, the factor that converts the relative uncertainty of an input into the relative uncertainty of the result, is 0.5, and the pressure contribution to the relative uncertainty of flow is 1 percent. The discharge coefficient, the factor that corrects the ideal orifice equation for friction and contraction of the jet, carries a relative standard uncertainty of 0.8 percent, and the fluid density carries a relative standard uncertainty of 0.4 percent. The combined standard uncertainty, the root-sum-of-squares combination of the contribution of each input, is 1.3 percent for the flow rate, and the absolute standard uncertainty of flow is 0.043 kilograms per second. A limiting check confirms the combination: with the pressure term removed, the combined value falls to 0.9 percent, and the fall matches the size of the pressure contribution in the full combination. The combination treats the three input uncertainties as independent, and a shared calibration source for two inputs breaks the treatment. A warning stands at the sensitivity step: the square root exponent applies to the differential pressure alone, and a coefficient applied to the density term inverts the density contribution. The stated uncertainty covers the meter at the stated operating point, and a new operating point takes a new propagation through the same steps.

points: Aim: a microneedle patch sensor that measures glucose in interstitial fluid continuously.
Method: 18 adults wore the patch for 14 days; readings every 5 minutes against paired venous reference samples.
Principal result: the sensor tracked the reference across the wearing period; mean absolute relative difference was 9.4 percent.
Paired readings in zone A of the consensus error grid: 96 percent; sensor lag behind blood glucose: 6 minutes.
definitions: interstitial fluid = fluid between cells, the fluid the patch samples
mean absolute relative difference = mean of the absolute difference between sensor and reference readings, divided by the reference reading, stated as a percentage
consensus error grid = grid that grades paired readings by the clinical consequence of the difference
prose: Diabetes management rests on frequent glucose readings, and fingerstick sampling gives a sparse record between meals and overnight. This study reports a microneedle patch sensor that measures glucose in interstitial fluid, the fluid between cells, continuously, and the study aim is a sensor record dense enough to carry the daily glucose profile. A group of 18 adults wore the patch for 14 days, with the patch recording every 5 minutes against paired venous reference samples. The sensor tracked the reference across the wearing period, and the mean absolute relative difference, the mean of the absolute difference between sensor and reference readings divided by the reference reading, was 9.4 percent. Paired readings in zone A of the consensus error grid, the grid that grades paired readings by the clinical consequence of the difference, reached 96 percent, and the sensor lag behind blood glucose was 6 minutes. The lag matches the physiological delay between blood and interstitial fluid, and a record at the stated difference from the reference is a candidate input for closed-loop dosing studies. The patch record covers meals, sleep, and exercise in daily life as worn.

points: Aim: a kinetic promoter that shortens the induction time of methane hydrate formation in a stirred reactor.
Method: reactor at 8.5 megapascals and 276 kelvin; promoter concentration 0.5 grams per litre; 12 runs at each condition.
Principal result: induction time fell from 210 minutes in pure water to 45 minutes with the promoter, a reduction of 78.6 percent.
Gas uptake reached a storage capacity of 138 volumes of gas per volume of hydrate.
definitions: induction time = time from pressurisation to the first detectable hydrate crystal growth
kinetic promoter = additive that shortens the induction time without entering the hydrate structure
storage capacity = volumes of gas, stated at standard conditions, held in a unit volume of hydrate
methane hydrate = ice-like solid of water cages holding methane molecules
prose: Methane hydrate, an ice-like solid of water cages holding methane molecules, stores gas at high density, and slow formation limits hydrate-based gas storage. This study examines a kinetic promoter, an additive that shortens the induction time without entering the hydrate structure, in a stirred reactor, and the study aim is a formation cycle short enough for a daily storage duty. The reactor ran at 8.5 megapascals and 276 kelvin, with a promoter concentration of 0.5 grams per litre and 12 runs at each condition. The induction time, the time from pressurisation to the first detectable hydrate crystal growth, fell from 210 minutes in pure water to 45 minutes with the promoter, a reduction of 78.6 percent, and gas uptake reached a storage capacity of 138, the storage capacity being the volumes of gas at standard conditions held in a unit volume of hydrate. Fast nucleation at the stated uptake places the formation step inside a daily charge and discharge cycle, and hydrate storage at the stated induction time is a candidate for buffer storage at gas processing sites. The promoter stays in the water phase across cycles, and the water phase carries the promoter into the next charge.

points: Established quality measures at the point of use: resistivity 18.2 megaohm centimetres and total organic carbon below 1 microgram per litre.
Particle specification: fewer than 10 particles per litre larger than 0.05 micrometres.
Gap: boron in product water reaches 0.02 micrograms per litre before the ion exchange beds show exhaustion on the standard measures, and the boron profile across a bed cycle is unmeasured.
definitions: ultrapure water = water purified to a resistivity near the theoretical limit of water, with ionic and organic contaminants at microgram per litre levels or below
resistivity = electrical resistance of a water sample normalised to a unit cube, the standard purity measure for ultrapure water
total organic carbon = mass of organically bound carbon per litre of water
point of use = last point in the distribution loop before the water reaches a process tool
limits: The study covers a single fabrication plant polishing loop.
prose: Semiconductor fabrication rinses wafers in ultrapure water at every lithography step, and water quality at the point of use sets a floor on defect density. Ultrapure water is water purified to a resistivity near the theoretical limit of water, with ionic and organic contaminants at microgram per litre levels or below, and the point of use is the last point in the distribution loop before the water reaches a process tool. Plant control rests on two established measures: resistivity, the electrical resistance of a water sample normalised to a unit cube, held at 18.2 megaohm centimetres, and total organic carbon, the mass of organically bound carbon per litre of water, held below 1 microgram per litre, with a particle specification of fewer than 10 particles per litre larger than 0.05 micrometres. Boron escapes the standard measures: boron in product water reaches 0.02 micrograms per litre before the ion exchange beds show exhaustion on resistivity or on total organic carbon, and the boron profile across a bed cycle is a missing piece of knowledge. The study aim is a boron record across the full bed cycle at the point of use, in a single fabrication plant polishing loop. The method places a boron analyser at the point of use and a second analyser at the polishing loop outlet, and sampling runs across two bed cycles.

points: Reference starch formulation at a feed moisture of 16 percent, a barrel temperature of 150 degrees Celsius, and a screw speed of 300 revolutions per minute gives an expansion ratio of 3.4 and a hardness of 28 newtons.
definitions: expansion ratio = diameter of the extrudate divided by the diameter of the die opening
hardness = peak force in a compression test on the extrudate, in newtons
twin-screw extruder = cooker with two intermeshing screws that convey, mix, and heat the feed
limits: The reference values cover the starch formulation in the stated operating window.
prose: Food extrusion cooks and shapes cereal and protein products in a single pass, and texture is the property a buyer grades first. A twin-screw extruder, a cooker with two intermeshing screws that convey, mix, and heat the feed, gives an expansion ratio of 3.4 and a hardness of 28 newtons for a reference starch formulation at a feed moisture of 16 percent, a barrel temperature of 150 degrees Celsius, and a screw speed of 300 revolutions per minute. prose: The biomass concentration N, in grams per litre, is the central quantity of the logistic growth relation for a microbial culture in a batch vessel. prose: The array trial supports a bounded claim: a 3 turbine array at 5 rotor diameters spacing delivers a capacity factor near the single-turbine value at the same site, at the tested site conditions, with array interaction as the measured penalty. Availability, the share of a period in which a turbine stands ready to generate, was 94 percent of the trial period, and availability losses and wake losses, the wake being the slowed flow downstream of a turbine rotor, account for the full gap between the array value and the baseline. Two evidence strands combine in the claim: the generation record sets the capacity factor, and the availability record separates downtime from flow interaction. The claim carries its limits. The trial covers one site with a tidal range up to 6 metres, and a full annual cycle of biofouling growth was not covered. Spacing below the tested value, and sites with a stronger directional spread in the flow, sit outside the tested scope. Maintenance visits were grouped into neap-tide windows, and no visit required a rotor lift during the trial. Marine growth on the blades was photographed at each visit and graded against the same photographic scale.
